#5716. U.S. on the Verge of Forfeiting Major Public Health Victory on Measles

— The nation is having its worst measles year in decades

International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories -- the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus' spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past 2 years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico -- that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.

"It's a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards," said David Margolius, MD, director of Cleveland's health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.

Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

International Health Experts Are Poring Over Measles Data This Week

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for 1 year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.

"It's solely based on genetics," said Amesh Adalja, MD, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have "eliminated" measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.

The CDC Says Loss of Measles Elimination Status Won't Change Its Approach

A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, said this week.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we're working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks," she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and has lauded Trump's executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups' recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

The U.S. Is Having Its Worst Measles Year in Decades

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine -- which is credited with saving millions of lives globally -- is possibly "quite lethal." Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah, and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year -- more than any year in more than three decades -- and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

At Least 50 People Have Died From Measles in Mexico

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed -- in 1963, in the U.S. -- and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.

As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.

#5715. Ask a Scientist: Who Has a Voice in Clean Air Protections?

If developers and planners decide to site an industrial chemical plant next door to your home, you’d want the chance to speak up about it. Soliciting input from the communities and individuals affected by pollution is an essential part of how environmental and public health laws are enforced. Under the federal Clean Air Act, large polluting facilities like power plants, chemical manufacturers, and refineries need to have a building permit, and every permitting decision must go through a “notice and comment” process. Although this is a federal law, it’s largely implemented by state, regional, and local agencies. And as a new UCS analysis shows, how much influence people have on the air permitting process varies greatly depending on where they live.

Darya Minovi leads fair access research for the Center for Science and Democracy at UCS. She is the lead author of Community Access to Clean Air Decisionmaking: Analysis of State Engagement in Title V Permitting, a new report that looks state-by-state at how people can make their voices heard.

AAS: What inspired you to do this analysis?

Darya Minovi: Last year, our team did an analysis of how the Trump administration is limiting public input on regulations andalso developed a set of recommendations for how government agencies should ensure the public gets to participate. With the administration very clearly side-stepping or ignoring these public processes, we did not, to put it lightly, expect the federal government to be a willing recipient of our research and guidance.

During the Biden administration, the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) did a lot of work to assess and expand meaningful public participation in government decisions. That was essentially all thrown away when President Trump was inaugurated. After consulting with colleagues and partners, we wanted to know: in this vacuum where the federal government isn’t interested in making progress, could we work with states to advance the public’s ability to participate in environmental policies?

AAS: Why does this participation matter, and how did you end up focusing on the air pollution permitting process?

DM: When you look at the core principles of environmental justice, meaningful engagement is central. People have the right to understand what’s happening in their communities and ideally be part of shaping those decisions. They need the opportunity to speak out and be respectfully listened to. People’s lived experience is expertise that can and should inform policy decisions. That’s democracy in action. At the federal level, environmental justice has been targeted and dismantled, but some states still value these

One specific environmental program where public participation is relevant is in Title V of the federal Clean Air Act (CAA), which covers operating permits for facilities that generate air pollution. This includes power plants, refineries, trash incinerators, and factories that manufacture chemicals—under the law, these are often called “major sources,” and there are very specific legal requirements about public participation. It’s one of the main ways air pollution gets regulated. But even though CAA is a federal law, it’s largely state and local agencies that carry out this permit process.

When a facility owner or company wants to apply for a permit to operate, they must submit a permit application to the relevant state, regional, or local agency. The agency writes a draft permit, which must be posted publicly in some way. The CAA requires agencies to accept public comments on the draft permit for at least 30 days and, if requested by the public, hold a hearing. Agencies also have a legal obligation to respond to substantive comments. These are very clear steps laid out in the law. It’s a high bar for participation, but we wanted to better understand how it works in practice.

What we found in our analysis is that the agencies with the authority to issue permits will approve Title V air permits unless there’s some clear problem with legal compliance. But the public can use that “notice and comment” process to slow down and influence what the facility will actually be permitted to do.

However, some agencies treat the public comment process as a set of boxes to check off. The law isn’t specific about meaningful engagement practices beyond public comment, so our analysis also looked at practices, programs, guidance, and laws at the state level, beyond what’s required by the federal government to enhance public participation in air permitting.

AAS: How did you do this analysis, and what did you find?

DM: We wanted to get the answers to three big questions.

We started with what I’ll call “desktop research”—reviewing agency websites and laws as though we were residents looking to navigate the process. All 50 states do have at least a website with some information. In general, agencies are posting draft permits and accepting public comments, as the CAA requires. But there are big differences in how that happens.

Public hearings aren’t very frequent and usually happen only if there’s a critical mass of people demanding them. We also reviewed nearly 90 permits from 35 different states—the public notices are often very technical, not easily readable by a layperson, and they’ll say things like “comments are due 30 days from posting date” instead of giving the actual dated deadline.

Very few states translate these notices into languages other than English. And we assessed whether the notices use “plain language” best practices—defining scientific terms, using white space and bullet points—and found that most states aren’t integrating these effectively. Minnesota and Michigan stand out as providing clear, readable information, and that’s largely the result of advocacy by local groups there.

We found that while 42 states had some resources describing how people can participate in permitting, the quality varied significantly. By and large permitting webpages and resources seem better designed for regulated industries, not the general public.

Ultimately, a public notice is only useful if you can find it, read it, and understand what it means and what you’re supposed to do to get involved!

We also wanted to know: do the comments make a difference? If they’re just going to get collected and sit on a shelf, that’s less meaningful than if agencies answer them or make actual changes to the permit in response. It’s very rare for agencies to deny a permit, but there are ways for public comments to have an impact—correcting errors, adding monitoring requirements, and strengthening enforcement.

AAS: You reached out to states to learn more. What did you find?

DM: Talking directly to these state agencies was an important part of our research. We built an 88-question survey, based on our September 2025 guidance, to ask agencies how they provide information, what they do to encourage participation, and what resources they have to carry the work out.

While we sent that survey to every state, only half the states responded in full, with 3 more responding partially. A few states said they intended to respond but didn’t, while others declined to participate or failed to respond entirely. That itself speaks to the capacity and, perhaps, interest these agencies have.

The states’ answers varied. Of the 28 states we heard back from, only 18 said they post responses to comments online, and only 13 could give us an example of when public comments resulted in a change to a permit.

At least 11 states have laws that go beyond what’s required in the CAA, and those laws often center environmental justice or cumulative impacts. States with these laws tended to have more readily available information on how to participate, as well as more resources and funding devoted to public outreach. Having these laws—or at least guidelines—in place does seem to create agency-wide changes to enhance public engagement.

Meaningful engagement takes time, money, and actual staff to manage the process. Only 20 of the agencies we spoke to provide training on public participation or environmental justice for staff, and only 16 have actual full-time staff dedicated to the process.

Unfortunately, the federal government is pushing in the opposite direction. Aaron Szabo, the (now former) director of the air-quality office at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, issued a memo urging states to expedite the Title V permitting process and rapidly review permits—saying explicitly that agencies don’t get many comments, so they don’t really matter.

DM: I was surprised by how much variability there was between and even within states. Some might have a lot of resources explaining how to participate in air permitting, but it’s a confusing website. Others might translate public notices in other languages but have no other information about how to participate.

While there’s a lot of room for improvement, there are some instructive examples too. For example, North Dakota has explicit guidance on how to write an effective public comment, with examples of common mistakes to avoid. Connecticut and Wisconsin have specific “how to” webpages to help people make comments or request a hearing. South Carolina has a webpage specifically entitled “Air Quality Decisions” that lays out what decision was made and posts the comments made in response to the draft permit. Ohio was the only state that got an “A” grade for readability of a public notice, with most states falling in the B/C range.

Every state can do better, of course, and we have a set of recommendations for how these agencies can improve. Governors, state lawmakers, and agency heads have a role to play here—certainly with funding for agencies and laws, but also in how they direct their agencies to carry this process out. Using public health data, translating notices into culturally appropriate languages and presenting them in plain language, making sure there’s fulltime staff devoted to public participation—these are just some of the steps to make participating in the air permitting process more meaningful, so that people not only have their voices heard, but actually have influence on decisions that shape air quality in their communities.

Courtesy of The Equation, UCS. By Seth D. Michaels.

#5714. More Bugatti Customers Should Spec Polished Engine Covers, But They're All Too Chicken

When you're buying a multi-million-dollar hypercar like a Bugatti Mistral, there are countless options to choose from even before you start getting into the really bespoke stuff. Selecting your paint shade, upholstery scheme, wheel design and stitching color is just the tip of the iceberg — for instance, on the Mistral, you can replace the elephant sculpture in the shifter with something else, like a mini Statue of Liberty or a screw from a 100-year-old Bugatti, as two customers have done.

There is one option that only a tiny handful of Bugatti owners have gone for, and it's a real shame: the polished engine covers. Almost every modern Bugatti since the Veyron has had their engine bays exposed to the elements, and many buyers get the W16's engine covers painted in a matching or contrasting color, or maybe one of a dozen carbon-fiber finishes, instead of the regular gunmetal. The polished aluminum option is very expensive, but that's not what deters Bugatti customers from optioning it. No, they're just too wimpy.

This is a take I've freely said for a long time now, but it came to the forefront of my mind when I was at the 2026 Las Vegas Concours a couple weekends ago. While there wasn't a lineup of 47 Veyrons like last year, there were 20 modern Bugattis on display, including the Mistral you see here that has the polished engine covers on its W16. I'm not usually one to gush over black cars but it's a pretty nice spec, and those magnesium wheels are another rare option.

The engine covers, though! Aren't they fantastic? That's how they look on a cloudy day, too, and are eye-catching even from a lower angle like that. Despite looking so awesome, fewer than 5% of buyers have gone for the option, and Bugatti's designers have told me it's because they don't want the covers to get dirty and scratched. I think that's exactly why more people should get them! Who doesn't love a bit of patina on a high-end car? Just look at the photos of this 2022 Chiron Super Sport that sold on Bring a Trailer last year. Isn't it neat to see the bright, shiny engine covers all scuffed up?

It's hard to pin down Bugatti option prices, but looking at the Monroneys (auto nerd speak for window sticker) of other Chiron sale listings helps. On a 2022 Chiron Pur Sport getting the engine covers painted in bright Tangerine cost $8,800, while going for an exposed carbon-fiber finish, like the one you see above, was $12,500. The polished option? $40,700.

OK, yeah, that's a lot. I know you can afford it, though, because you're buying a Bugatti, and in the grand scheme of things, it's not even really expensive. The Chiron's Sky View roof, for instance, was $62,000, and going for an exposed carbon-fiber body would've set you back at least $300,000. So what's an extra forty grand to get such a gorgeous engine bay? We don't yet know whether the Tourbillon's V16 will offer a similar finish (we know it'll have a carbon engine bay option), but I hope it does — and hopefully a much larger percentage of the 250 buyers will go for it.

#5713. Your Holiday Gifts Don’t Have To Be Delivered By Diesel

The 2026 holiday shopping season is soon to be upon us, with gift buyers and bargain hunters perusing stores in person and online. Behind the scenes, the US freight system has been working hard to transport the goods and gifts, traveling mostly by truck as they make their way through ports, warehouses, and highways.

So, what effect will the rising price of gasoline and diesel fuel have on the year’s biggest shopping season? The historic shock in prices at the pump has driven cost increases for the goods consumers buy throughout the economy, including holiday gifts, because costs to produce and ship goods have increased. Between January and October, the average national price for a gallon of diesel rose nearly 80 percent.

But it doesn’t have to be this way. The trucks moving and delivering goods throughout the economy don’t have to be subject to the high cost and volatility of the fossil fuel market. Globally, businesses are transitioning their fleets to zero-emission trucks. In addition to their public health and environmental benefits, zero-emission trucks (and battery-electric models in particular) offer significant reductions in operating costs compared to those powered by fossil fuels. This can help protect producers and consumers from expensive and volatile fuel prices and unhealthy air.

That can help us all breathe a bit easier.

This year’s holiday shopping season is marked by several unsettling trends—record high fuel prices and the second-largest monthly jump in the Producer Price Index (PPI) since 2010, as well as the largest 12-month increase in the PPI since 2022. This jump in the PPI, the measure of the costs incurred by US businesses to make, ship, and sell their goods, was meaningfully driven by the single largest month-to-month increase in producer energy costs in the past decade and a half. Additionally, September 2026 saw the third largest increase in transportation and warehousing costs under the PPI since 2010, only behind April 2026 and March 2022—the months following the beginning of the current US-Iran conflict and Russia’s war on Ukraine, respectively.

While Santa’s reindeer are primarily fueled by carrot snacks during the holiday season, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, the rest of our nation’s freight system is most often powered by dirty and increasingly expensive fossil fuels. In September, diesel fuel prices hit record highs—topping as much as $9 per gallon at some retail gas stations. Diesel-fueled trucks are the workhorse of the US freight system, carrying more freight by weight than all other transportation modes combined. Each year, tractor trucks consume over 27 billion gallons of fuel, and fuel is the second-largest cost input to trucking after labor.

Higher fuel costs can ultimately be passed along to consumers and contribute to higher price variance for goods. This is particularly the case with certain food prices. A 2023 study in Energy Economics found that fuel price shocks accounted for nearly 20 percent of the price variance of cereals. Unfortunately, this means that even the reindeer aren’t immune to fossil fuel volatility.

Consumers may never see a fuel surcharge listed on a holiday gift, but fuel costs are embedded throughout the supply chain. When diesel prices spike, it becomes more expensive to move products between ports, warehouses, stores, and homes, even for carriers that hedge fuel prices through bulk or futures fuel agreements. Powering more of those trips with comparatively stable electricity can reduce one source of sudden cost pressure before products reach shopping carts.

Battery-electric trucks can provide far greater fuel cost predictability while also offering significantly lower per-mile fuel costs than fossil-fueled trucks. Between January 2016 and September 2026 (the most recent data month at the time of this publication), annual diesel price volatility averaged 3.75 times that of commercial electricity prices, according to our analysis of Federal Reserve and Energy Information Administration data. During this time, diesel prices saw a monthly spike of greater than 10 percent seven times, including four times in 2026. Diesel prices between February and March 2026 saw the highest price spike by far at over 32 percent. By contrast, the highest spike in the national average commercial electricity price in the last decade was 4.4 percent.

While it’s true that both diesel and electricity prices have increased this year, the magnitude of those increases is hardly comparable. Between January and September, the average national price for a gallon of diesel fuel rose nearly 80 percent compared to just two percent for average commercial electricity rates.

Consumers are paying for these higher petroleum prices at the pump and checkout lines, while oil companies and shareholders are seeing a windfall: both ExxonMobil’s and Chevron’s Q3 2026 earnings were more than double those of Q3 2025.

But the costs of our fossil fuel-powered freight system extend far beyond our wallets.

Fossil-fueled medium- and heavy-duty trucks are also the nation’s largest source of smog-forming pollution and account for the largest share of the nearly 10,000 premature deaths associated with transportation pollution in the US each year, despite making up just 13 percent of the vehicles on our roads.

Trucks are a particularly significant source of pollution in areas near the warehouses and logistics centers that our holiday packages travel through. For the 66 million people living near freight corridors, warehouses, ports, and railyards nationwide, the price of a fossil fuel-powered freight system is too often paid for with their health. Recent UCS research found that the 1.7 million people living near 10 or more freight facilities face a cancer risk from air toxics that is 32 percent higher than the national average.

While freight operators cannot control geopolitics and fuel prices, they can control which fuels they choose to use. Increasingly, freight operators are considering the switch to electric trucks, which offer more stable and affordable fueling costs with far less exposure to volatile global oil markets. FedEx, for example, recently announced plans to add 2,000 electric delivery trucks to its growing zero-emission delivery fleet.

The economics for zero-emission trucks are increasingly compelling—this is partially why we’ve seen continued adoption of electric commercial vehicles despite the current federal leadership’s best efforts to prolong our reliance on fossil fuels. Even states not typically thought of as electrification front-runners have seen meaningful growth in zero-emission delivery vehicles. In 2025, over 17 percent of new commercial vans in both Mississippi and Louisiana were zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs). In Georgia, nearly 35 percent of new commercial vans registered last year were electric.

California continues to lead the nation in overall deployments of zero-emission medium-and-heavy-duty vehicles, with zero-emission models accounting for over 24 percent of all new vehicle registrations in 2025. While this is a slight backstep from 2024 levels, California continues to see growth in the deployment of zero-emission tractor trucks. In California, ZEVs comprise around 8 percent of new tractor trucks registered in 2025, and it appears the momentum is just getting started. In the first three quarters of 2026 alone, California fleets applied for state clean truck incentives for more than 1,000 new electric tractor trucks—a clear example of growing interest and demand.

Momentum toward tractor truck electrification is picking up in other parts of the country as well. In September, Catalyst Mobility, a leading clean transportation nonprofit, announced that a group of major businesses, including Microsoft and Pepsi, placed a combined order for 2,500 battery-electric Tesla Semis—the largest single order of zero-emission trucks in US history. These trucks can travel up to 500 miles on a single charge at maximum legal capacity and regain 60 percent of range in a 30-minute charge. Earlier this year, Pilot Travel Centers announced a partnership with Tesla to install high-speed chargers for electric semi-trucks across major freight corridors in California, Georgia, Nevada, New Mexico, and Texas. The first of these stations is now operational.

Despite impressive momentum, private investments and market forces alone are unlikely to reliably electrify our freight system at the needed pace. The freight industry continues to face widespread adoption barriers, including higher upfront costs for many zero-emission truck models and lack of access to widespread, reliable commercial truck charging infrastructure. At the same time, consumers have limited ability to choose shippers committed to cleaner freight. We cannot simply toggle a “green delivery” option when shopping at a local store or online.

That’s where public policy comes in: to reduce barriers to electric truck adoption and accelerate the transition toward a cleaner, more affordable freight system.

At a time when the federal government’s support for freight sustainability and modernization has reversed and is undermining previous progress, state and local governments have the opportunity and responsibility to adopt and implement policies and programs that build momentum toward an electrified freight system. Specifically, they should accelerate zero-emission truck deployment where it is technically and economically feasible today, while addressing the technological and economic barriers that limit adoption elsewhere.

Policies and programs that drive electrification today while addressing barriers could include those that:

This holiday season, millions of gifts will move through a vast network of trucks, warehouses, and distribution centers before we give them to friends and loved ones. Increasingly, those trucks don’t have to run on diesel. Electric trucks offer a path toward a freight system that produces less pollution while reducing business and consumer exposure to the volatile global fossil fuel market.

However, widescale freight electrification is unlikely to occur at the pace needed without effective public policy. Smart public policies and programs can accelerate electric truck deployment where it already makes the most economic and environmental sense, while tackling the costs and infrastructure challenges that remain.

Consumers don’t always have the option or transparency to choose cleaner freight, but we can push our elected representatives to pursue policies and programs that deliver a more sustainable way to move the economy.

If you’re an early-career scientist, seasoned scientist, or technical expert, you can join our science network for opportunities to advocate for smarter transportation policies.

Courtesy of The Equation, UCS. By Sam Wilson.

#5712. 'Worst Possible News': Cybertruck Fans Melt Down After Tesla Cancels Its Wheeled Electric Dumpster

As anyone with even a passive knowledge of our existence could have told you, Elon Musk's announcement that Tesla will kill the Cybertruck next year was big news here at Jalopnik. After three-ish years, we finally defeated our mortal enemy. The Cybertruck will die, and Jalopnik still lives. Of course, you had to know there'd be at least a few die-hard Cybertruck fans who chugged the Kool-Aid and may have cried when they heard the news. Thankfully, our friends over at Wired tracked down many of the more enjoyable meltdowns, purely for your entertainment.

Before we dive too deep into the a few examples, though, can we just take a second to appreciate how perfectly Wired journalist Miles Klee summed up the Cybertruck's woes? It's beautiful:

Automotive industry observers were quick to surmise that the vehicle's weak sales, delayed deliveries, inflated pricing, numerous recalls, and connection to Musk's far-right MAGA politics may also have factored into the decision. Longtime detractors of the polarizing steel-paneled truck, originally positioned as an electric rival to classic gas-powered pickups, jeered Musk and Tesla fans over its demise, noting with some pleasure that the Cybertruck would exit the market within four years of its November 2023 rollout.

I don't get the feeling he's one of those Cybertruck fans left brokenhearted following the cancellation announcement, which is good. Miles gets an invite to my upcoming Cybertruck Is Dead cookout next year. Anyway, onto the schadenfreude. Here's a thread he found from a Cybertruck owners' forum that you'll definitely want to scroll through. "Worst possible news," one poster wrote, adding, "No chance to buy another in future years for a newer model or after a car accident. No more aftermarket mods. No more service or parts."

Don't be too mean to that commenter, though. Those aftermarket parts are important when you own a truck that loses body panels like a toddler loses socks. In their world, maybe it really is the worst possible news. Meanwhile, another Cybertruck owner who goes by the name The Cybertruck Guy on Twitter posted, "I... have no words. Devastating. I can't help but think this is Tesla's own unwillingness (or incompetence) to make Cybertruck a success. Where was the price cuts? Where were the advertisements? Where is range extender? Where is the future of autonomous cargo transport?"

I… have no words. Devastating.I can’t help but think this is Tesla’s own unwillingness (or incompetence) to make Cybertruck a success. Where was the price cuts? Where were the advertisements? Where is range extender? Where is the future of autonomous cargo transport?

In addition to highlighting a few of the best sad reactions, Wired also spoke with Cybertruck fans to hear their thoughts directly. "So everybody in my group, they are not happy," a contractor in Palm Springs name Michael Goldman told Wired. "I've had people reaching out to me through the group, asking me, like, 'What are you going to do?' And I'm like, 'Dude, I don't know.'" That group, by the way, is called Cybertruck Owners Only and has more than 82,000 members, every single one of whom we can assume is equally depressed now.

The article also uses the "betrayal" and "disappointment" to describe how many owners feel, which always feels good to see. As for Goldman, he told Wired he nearly bought a second Cybertruck to have for when his first one dies. Unfortunately for Mr. Goldman here, that didn't work out because Tesla pulled the ultimate Tesla move on him right before he pulled the trigger. "I'll be honest with you, I was going pull the trigger on a [Cyberbeast] about two days ago, and I have a reservation already in my phone," Goldman told Klee. But before he officially put his order in, "the price increased like another $8,000 or something, and that was my sign to not do it."

That price increase wasn't personal, though. Per Car and Driver, while the Cybertruck will reportedly stay in production through some point in 2027, the only version you can now buy costs $112,000. So that's not exactly cheap. Then again, who expects consistent pricing out of Tesla? You may not have to negotiate with a dealer salesperson, but Tesla pricing is still an expensive game of Russian roulette, and it has been for years.

Speaking with Wired, Troy Meekhof (the man behind the Cybertruck Guy Twitter account) said, "I absolutely do think this is the wrong move for the Tesla brand, and it's not necessarily because of the removal of an under-performing product, but it's a clear symbol of Tesla's aggression towards transitioning to autonomous vehicles only," adding, "If you ask me, it is far too aggressive, and I have a growing conviction that, at least in America, the population and legislators are not ready nor interested in autonomous vehicles today en masse." Huh.

Why Meekhof would feel disappointed to see Tesla abandon vehicle production as it pursues its AI/robotics future, I have no idea. We've known that was the plan since 2024, when Elon literally told us that was the plan. While Musk is a proven liar with a long track record of saying he'll do things he never does, his actions since making that announcement have only demonstrated a willingness to pursue his plan, which also involves attempting to merge Tesla with SpaceX. Elon killed both the Model S and Model X back in January, too.

Then again, that's the problem with thinking you're special. You can look at Tesla cutting everything that isn't the Model 3 or Model 3 hatchback, refusing to redesign its product, and killing the long-rumored $25,000 "cheap Tesla," and you'll still assume Elon will keep building his slow-selling truck just for you and your Cybertruck-driving friends. Being forced to face the reality that they aren't Elon's favorite customers who are basically his best friends has apparently been rough for some of these guys.

Cybertruck Owners Only groupmember Drew Million told Wired, "I've lost a lot of love for Tesla over this," before complaining about the electric automaker's "very stale consumer options." Million also added, "After Cybertruck is gone, there isn't a flagship vehicle. The Cybertruck started that," apparently still confused about whether or not Tesla is still a car company. And while you'd think Meekhof's claim that Tesla shouldn't go all-in on (very, very flawed) robotaxis would be rare among Tesla owners, it may not be. From Wired:

It's a point that comes up again and again from Tesla boosters protesting the sunset of the Cybertruck: They don't want to give up their own independence in favor of robot chauffeurs. An owner wrote on X, for example, that they didn't understand Tesla's push "to delete the steering wheel, the pedals, the ownership, the freedom of having a vehicle" with the Cybercab, which cannot accommodate an entire family. They lamented that the company "doesn't seem to want to continue innovating in the customer car segment.

There is, of course, plenty of additional schadenfreude to enjoy, so if you like what you've read so far, head on over to Wired to give the whole thing a read. It's more than worth your time, I promise.

#5711. Alzheimer's Study Tracks Faster Tau Buildup in Younger Patients

— Tau spread more rapidly across a wider area of the brain in early-onset Alzheimer's disease

People with early-onset Alzheimer's disease had faster and more severe accumulation of tau than those whose Alzheimer's symptoms started after age 65, imaging data showed.

Compared with older Alzheimer's patients, tau burden was higher in younger patients and spread more rapidly across a wider area of the brain, reported Konstantinos Chiotis, MD, PhD, of the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and co-authors.

Early-onset Alzheimer's patients also had stronger correlations between tau buildup, amyloid-beta accumulation, and broader cognitive decline, Chiotis and colleagues wrote in Science Translational Medicine.

"Younger patients had substantially more tau even after accounting for differences in clinical severity," Chiotis said in a statement. "Their tau also accumulated faster over time. Delayed diagnosis alone does not explain this pattern."

The study compared baseline and longitudinal tau in 390 early-onset Alzheimer's patients with a mean age of 59, and 211 late-onset patients with a mean age of 78. It is the largest to compare tau in both early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease.

"The results confirm that early-onset Alzheimer's disease seems to advance faster both biologically and clinically," Nicolai Franzmeier, PhD, of Ludwig Maximilians University in Munich, who wasn't involved with the study, told MedPage Today. This considerably strengthens previous evidence that linked younger age at symptom onset to more extensive tau pathology, Franzmeier noted.

Early-onset disease accounts for approximately 5% of all Alzheimer's cases, though some studies suggest young-onset forms of Alzheimer's and other dementias may be more common than once thought.

"Patients with early-onset Alzheimer's are more likely than older patients to present with symptoms unrelated to memory, at least initially," co-author Renaud La Joie, PhD, of the University of California San Francisco, said in a statement. "They might have difficulty interpreting what they are seeing despite a normal eye exam. They might struggle with judging distances and may have trouble reading," he added.

"Some patients may experience a decline in language abilities in which they have difficulty retrieving words and following long sentences, although speech remains fluent," La Joie pointed out. "Others may struggle with executive functioning, such as attention, problem-solving, planning, and adapting to changing situations."

It's not clear why early-onset Alzheimer's disease develops, the researchers noted. To compare early- and late-onset Alzheimer's patients, Chiotis and colleagues studied adults with confirmed amyloid pathology, mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, and tau PET measured with 18F-flortaucipir. A subset of participants had follow-up imaging over 2 to 3 years.

Early-onset patients were from the Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study (LEADS) cohort. Late-onset patients were from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) repository.

The early-onset group had a higher proportion of women compared with the late-onset group (55% vs 42%) and more participants diagnosed with dementia at baseline (72% vs 36%). Nearly one in five early-onset patients had a non-amnestic presentation, while 99.25% of late-onset patients had memory problems.

At baseline, the early-onset group had higher amyloid PET binding and more severe impairment across global cognitive measures, including Mini-Mental State Examination and Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes scores. Over time, early-onset patients accumulated tau tangles faster in every region of interest.

"Although early-onset Alzheimer's disease participants also showed higher amyloid-beta PET burden, the differences in amyloid-beta were substantially smaller than those observed in tau PET burden, consistent with neuropathological studies showing greater differences in tau than in amyloid-beta burden between early-onset Alzheimer's disease and late-onset Alzheimer's disease," Chiotis and co-authors noted.

Co-pathologies were not directly assessed in the study, and their contribution to differences between early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease remains uncertain, the researchers acknowledged.

Young-onset dementia patients can have diagnostic delays which may affect employment, financial security, and family needs, and postpone support and care.

"We need greater awareness of Alzheimer's in younger adults and better access to specialist assessment, including tau PET when clinically appropriate," Chiotis said. "These scans show how much tau pathology is present and where it is located, helping us understand unusual symptoms and how far the disease has progressed biologically."

#5709. Hydropower Generation in the Southwest Fell to Record Lows This Summer

Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows.

However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years.

We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won’t eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity.

According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region’s generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.

Article from Today in Energy. Principal contributor: Lindsay Aramayo.

The EIA collects, analyzes, and disseminates independent and impartial energy information to promote sound policymaking, efficient markets, and public understanding of energy and its interaction with the economy and the environment.

#5708. How The Developers Of '007 First Light' Nailed The Feeling Of Being James Bond Through Its Cars And Vehicles

As a massive fan of the James Bond franchise, my main hope going into "007 First Light" wasn't that it would have characters and plot points I recognized or have all the right bits of fan service — I just wanted the game to evoke the same emotions that the Bond movies do, to really feel like I was being Bond when playing. Luckily the game delivered those feelings in spades. IO Interactive, best known for the "Hitman" franchise, created one of the best pieces of James Bond media ever, and a big part of "First Light's" success is down to the vehicles you get to drive as Bond and how they're woven into the main story.

To learn more about the game's development, and the creation of the new DLC missions that feature the Aston Martin Valhalla, I hopped on a call with Rasmus Poulsen, the game's art director, and Dominic Vega, audio director and game director of live content/missions. "We knew from the get-go that we wanted as wide a range of driving experiences as we could manage to squeeze in the game, and of course that means everything from the unexpected to the hoped for," said Poulsen, and man did they deliver.

SPOILER ALERT: While I won't be talking about major plot or character spoilers in this story, I do spoil all of the various vehicular scenes and moments, so if you haven't played or finished the game yet, bookmark this page and come back to it later.

The first excellent car moment comes in one of the very first missions, when Bond is going through initial training to join the reborn 00 program. At a facility in Malta, Bond gets thrown the keys to a 2006 Aston Martin DBS, the same car seen in "Casino Royale" and "Quantum of Solace." It's described as "a classic" by one of Bond's compatriots, who adds it's "seen some real-life action too back in her day. Still a gorgeous drive." She's not lying — the DBS is totally banged up, covered in duct tape and zip ties.

Bond proceeds to race around a course, smashing through boxes and jumping down staircases. Despite how realistic the cars look and sound the handling is definitely on the arcade side of things, but it's also very fun. You're encouraged to do handbrake turns and always keep the throttle pinned, and enough actual skill and good driving is needed to do well in this mission and subsequent ones.

It's not a very long sequence, with Bond quickly moving on to other parts of training, but it's a great way to get us car people excited at the beginning of the game. This particular choice of car this early on is a great nod to our outgoing Bond on the silver screen, too. Bond movies have always had car chases, but it wasn't until the Daniel Craig films that the chases really leveled up, becoming grittier and more realistic and more exciting, sometimes the most blockbuster-y set pieces in the entire movie.

A few missions later, Bond and his fellow 00 trainees have to infiltrate a chess tournament at the Grand Carpathian Hotel in Slovakia, and they drive up in a 2007 Jaguar XJ, with Bond dressed as a chauffeur. This is where the game really nails the Bond feeling, with the regular cars and seemingly mundane scenes, and it was this aspect of putting cars in the game that Poulsen and Vega enjoyed the most. "The Bond franchise is not only about the low end and the high end, it's also about the sleeper cars. It's about getting the car people to go, 'I see you,' and it's for us to go, 'we see you too.' The middle of the pack there is really exciting to me," Poulsen said.

"Each of the Bond movies, the best ones, are a cohort of bands. Think of the curation of the cast of vehicles in the movie," Vega added. "We're making an 18-hour experience, we want to make sure that the cast of vehicles gets the nod [from fans]. It gets the 'ah OK, I see what you're doing there, oh you're doing a twist here, oh it's 'Living Daylights.'" The development team was in contact with Aston Martin and Jaguar Land Rover from the very beginning, and they knew they wanted to include a big variety of cars. "There's partnerships that you have to do with Bond, right, it's not Bond without certain vehicles in the mix, but then you still always want to surprise, you want to 'and' the expectation. The player should absolutely have their fantasy met, 'and'. I think it's really nice when people in the car world notice that," he said.

In the Slovakia scene, the player calmly drives the XJ down a winding mountain road toward the hotel. You don't drive fast, or take any shortcuts, or go off the set path; it's all about setting a scene. While driving the XJ, Bond and his crew are talking about the mission and giving you more backstory, like in a transitional movie scene. Instead of making something like this a cutscene, "First Light" lets you act it out. It's like the vehicular equivalent of a "walk and talk," if you know your movie-biz slang. You can take your time on the drive, which is especially nice now that a photo mode has been added to the game. (Everything you see in this story was captured by yours truly.) With how much of the game is straight-up action, it's really nice to have these moments of levity in between that add more depth to the characters.

Poulsen says the development team visited the JLR headquarters in Gaydon, getting tours of the heritage collection and its restoration facility, to figure out what vehicles they might want to use in the game. There was everything from classics to prototypes and rarities like the XJ220, plus things that aren't even out yet. "We walked around discussing, 'hmm, we need something that's not what gets the front page, what is it going to be?' We looked at the XJ of that particular year; it has a story of old money rather than flash, it's not so old that it's vintage, it's just in-between," Poulsen said. They pointed it out to Jaguar, saying "we want that one," and the company obliged. It is a perfect spec, too, one of the later facelifts in green over cream with those lovely five-spoke wheels.

Another part of the game sees Bond and his mentor heading to Mauritania, with the level starting off in a kitted-out Land Rover Defender. You get to drive the SUV across the gorgeous landscape, even doing some light rock crawling, before coming upon a city built inside of a ship graveyard that's run by the pirate king Bawma, played brilliantly by Lenny Kravitz. It's again used as a conversation piece, setting up the scenes to come. Bond gets back in the Defender for another exploring sequence a little later, and after a series of events including a lot more fighting, he gets rescued with the help of a great Series II pickup.

It's not all mundane drives, though. Later in the mission that starts with the XJ, after chaos ensues at the hotel, Bond has to chase after someone who's just hopped into a second-gen Jaguar XKR. He does so by breaking into and hotwiring a Bahama Yellow 1970 Aston Martin DBS, the same model used in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" (and the same color as the DBS from "The Persuaders"). There's a great moment of Bond cheekily flirting with a mysterious woman who hops into the car with him, and you're off.

Again, it's a pre-set route, but there are a bunch of fun shortcuts like swerving into a muddy field to avoid logging trucks, jumping over canals and driving through a farmer's market. You have to avoid other traffic and contend with other obstacles, and it can actually be a little tough at times. In one climactic moment, Bond drives the car onto and over a transport truck, using it as a ramp to get huge air. Who among us hasn't dreamt of doing that hundreds of times? Adding to the fun is a great damage model, with the DBS getting really beat up by the end of it even if you try and drive safely.

The car chase ends, but Bond is immediately thrust into a firefight at an airfield, which, of course, leads to him dodging explosions to hitch a ride on an escaping cargo plane. To do so, he takes control over one of those airport stair trucks, and jumps onto the wing of the plane. Then he fights a bunch of bad guys on the wing as the plane takes off, and eventually it leads to him freefalling from the plane, avoiding debris while trying to find a parachute — and you're in control pretty much the whole time. It's awesome, and really embodies that unique Bond feeling.

Like the "Hitman" games, "First Light" is all about using your environment to your advantage, and there's a lot of moments where a vehicle is part of that environment. In parts of the game where more baddies are arriving in cars, you can shoot at them, causing them to leak gas or oil and become easier to explode. Some vehicles can be hacked, with Bond able to set off car alarms or remotely activate gadgets like smoke screens. "Plenty of movies you see a car gadget that you never get to see [used in] the movie, so that was a little bit of a head nod there," Vega said.

The two best vehicular sequences in the game don't feature cars at all, though. Or at least not ones you're driving, since you do get to smash up plenty of others. At one point in the game, Bond escapes a gala by commandeering a garbage truck and wreaking havoc through the streets of London, and then later on he takes control of a giant mining truck and drives it through a quarry in Vietnam to, again, save his friends and escape the bad guys. While both sequences are small parts of much longer missions, they're absolute blasts to play through, some of my favorite moments of the game for sure, and they feel totally Bond. Just as you might realize, "oh hell yeah, I think Bond is gonna get in that tank" while watching one of the films, I was sitting on my couch thinking, "oh hell yeah, am I about to drive that thing?"

Vega said the two sequences came about in very different ways, with the mine truck being more organic. "The level's getting put together, and somebody puts a prop in, and then I think there is that incentive in game development, and especially in Bond, where you just want to say 'yes' to the player. Like you're rolling downhill, and someone throws something into the snowball, and instead of rejecting it you keep going." You see a bunch of these mining trucks earlier on in the mission, the game teasing what's about to come without you even knowing it yet. "The mining truck there being part of establishing the space, the place, and then ever so slightly you go, 'guys, well, let's go,' because you embody the mind of the character," Poulsen said of the scene being thought up on the fly.

"[That's the thing of First Light] being a catered experience. It's not open world, it's not everything, it's not all the vehicles; it's a specific subset of vehicles. That means it's interesting for us, that we can lure you forward with this truck and all these things, and have you go 'ah, yeah,' you got what you wanted. Rather than have a plethora of vehicles in front of you and you go 'OK, cool, which one?' No, the one we chose," said Poulsen. "You get what you wanted, but in a way that you wholly couldn't imagine or didn't imagine — unless you're a Bond fan, of course, in which case maybe you do imagine it."

The garbage truck, meanwhile, was a much longer road to get to. Vega talked about how resourcefulness is one of Bond's key character traits, one that differentiates him from other secret agent characters, and that's baked into the level designs from jump. Another one of Bond's best qualities is how he'll smash straight through an obstacle and keep on going. Which he does in this sequence quite a lot. "It was always in the script that he's going to get into this bin lorry in this really unexpected fashion. I think Craig embodied that, I think Brosnan had a bit of that, I think Dalton had a bit of that — put two dots on a map and draw a straight line, that's how James Bond got there, and that is a really cool moment of expression," Vega said.

What makes the garbage truck escape especially cathartic is how the mission starts: with an upset Bond sitting in traffic in a Range Rover SV, having a conversation with his boss. You can't even side-swipe traffic, with the game displaying a parking sensor warning on the screen and pulling the car back into the lane. "It's such a Londoner inside commentary there. He's frustrated, he's been told to stand down. We stick you in a powerful fantasy vehicle like the Land Rover and you can't open it up, you're just running errands. It's putting you in that headspace," said Vega, "so when we finally put you behind the wheel [of the garbage truck] an hour and a half later it's just like go go go go through the wall!"

One thing the game doesn't let Bond drive is what would traditionally be the hero car. In fact, the game rubs it in your face a bit. In a mission fairly early on in the game, you visit Q in his lab and have a conversation in front of a covered-up car that's being worked on by robots. The car is clearly the Aston Martin Valhalla to any slightly trained eye, and Q refuses to let Bond drive it even when it gets finished. He's not even a 00 yet, of course he's not getting to drive Q's souped-up supercar, and it's being built for a different agent anyway. "It kind of puts you in the shoes of Bond," said Vega, "who's like 'I wish you'd give me this on a mission!' That's always Q and Bond's relationship, it's a bit of restraint from Q where he gives you the gadgets you need, he's not giving you the keys to the castle."

Well, Bond will be Bond, so in one of the game's final missions, there's a scene where Bond gets those proverbial castle keys. To escape a siege on Q's lab he climbs into the Valhalla, fires up its machine guns and rockets, and does donuts around the room, killing bad guys and blowing basically everything up. You do actually get to control the car for this scene, but it's pretty brief, leading right into a cutscene that has a few comedic moments involving the car and its built-in voice assistant. It's a satisfying moment, since for hours after the Aston Martin is first seen, you've probably been thinking "man, I really hope we get to do something with the Valhalla."

The team began working on the game a little before the Valhalla was production-ready, receiving the CAD files from Aston so they could get started on it and figure out how to Bond-ify the car. "One of the artistic pillars for the project is that dichotomy between downplayed credibility and outlandish adventurous over-the-top-ness. We need to combine those two things," said Poulsen. Since the game uses a third-person camera view where you're looking forward from behind the character, and thus behind any vehicle, they decided against putting weapons in the headlights or front end of the car, where you wouldn't see them. The Valhalla has such a short, low front end there wasn't much to work with anyway. "We went with a design that would utilize the body and the shapes in an interesting way, and it made sense to put all the weaponry on the back," Poulsen said. "The principal concept artist did a bunch of designs with the CAD model, where we were experimenting with opening up the panels like a beetle or folding them in and out."

When they sent their ideas back to Aston, explaining the why and how behind their designs, the Aston team simply gave them the thumbs up. "Rather than being like 'no actually, you have a radiator there, and this and there's pipes and the thing and the valve,' they didn't give us a hard time because I think they could see that we had tried to some degree respect the negative space and interior space and all that stuff in the car," Poulsen said. The final design features the Valhalla's rear quarter panels opening out horizontally at an angle to reveal a giant auto-aiming machine gun mounted on an arm on each side. "We got that wonderful interplay and a really playful yet rather credible sense of weapons folding out. I'm sure it wouldn't necessarily be doable like this, but [Aston] didn't have a hard time with us wanting to do that, so it was a very smooth relationship."

That couldn't be it for the Valhalla, so the "First Light" team has released a few "Valhalla Protocol" time trial tactical simulation missions as DLC that let you really wring out the Valhalla on a newly designed course, either with or without weapons and obstacles engaged. When you're using the machine guns and rockets to take down obstacles, drones and other vehicles, it's definitely more outlandish than Bond movies usually are, but it fits right in with past Bond video games and reminds me of other excellent titles like "Spy Hunter." Even in strictly time trial mode it's pretty tough to achieve one of the best time targets, since you've still got to contend with all sorts of things on the road, like ramps that you obviously will want to jump off.

"At IO, we believe that shipping the game is the first step. We tell you the story we want to tell, but there's so much more that comes after that. We knew long, long ago that the best possible moment for the Valhalla was the climax of the techo-wizard experience. You've just done all this awesome stuff in Q lab, you see everything that Q built for you, it was always going to be racing around in donuts because you don't want to end that on a chase," Vega said. The final pursuit of the villain is very personal, so a climatic car chase wouldn't have felt right, but because the player now had Valhalla expectations from the start, Vega said they always planned to design post-launch content where you get to actually drive it.

It's a great redemption for the Valhalla, which has had a rough start to its time being featured in the Bond franchise. Aston revealed the concept version of the Valhalla in early 2019, and it originally played a bigger role in Craig's final Bond film, "No Time to Die," which started filming soon after the concept's reveal. That movie was supposed to come out in April 2020, but it ended up being delayed until September 2021 — a couple months after the production version of the Valhalla had been revealed, with a very different design and powertrain compared to the concept. In the final cut of the film, you briefly see the concept sitting in the background of Q's lab, and that's it.

As for what might make it into the next Bond movie, "First Light" could give us a little hint. In one scene when you're being escorted out of that ship graveyard by Bawma, Bond walks right past a bright blue Jaguar Type 00 concept. "Visiting the JLR design studio as a car nerd was just a dream come true, it was so cool, and we got to see the prototype of the Type 00, which was incredible," Poulsen said, "It was impressive to be there and see how that works. Walking past the clay model, it was just cool." JLR has provided Land Rovers and other cars to Bond movies for most of Craig's run, but I'm sure that its heavy involvement with "First Light" is a sign that it wants some new Jaguars to be featured in the next movies. I mean come on, can't you see James Bond driving the production Type 01? At least someone should, whether it's a villain or a Bond girl or hell, even M.

I couldn't get off the phone without asking Poulsen and Vega to tell me their favorite vehicular moments in the Bond film series, whether it be a major chase or a more nerdy throwaway moment. "I want to give a shoutout to the start of 'Quantum of Solace' just because it's so visceral and moody and cool," Poulsen said. "It's not as fun as the fun ones, it's more violent and hardcore, but damn that flows well. Or rather, it doesn't flow, it's much too staccato to flow, but ooh it's so good."

That is a great answer, but Vega holds the correct opinion, because his favorite is also my favorite. "Mine is 'GoldenEye,' but it's also because I think the dialogue plays such a role. It's a car chase where the villain is the Bond girl, but she's not having the conversation with him, he's having the conversation with the girl in the car," Vega said, referring to Bond's passenger, an MI6 employee named Caroline who is supposed to be psychologically investigating him. "I think it's the interplay; it's like a gunfight and it's a gadget fight and it's a car chase, all with just dialogue and driving. And it's low stakes, it's just having fun on the mountains. It's such an homage to the Bond girl outrunning Bond in a casual environment."

That's just one of a few great chases in that film. "The scale is so impressive, and it's the same thing [as the game] right, you go from high-precision handling, the fantasy of being the most capable person in the world, to driving a tank through a wall," Vega said, referring to one of "GoldenEye's" best moments. "I love the goofy vehicles of Bond a lot," he added. "I love the gondolas and I love the hovercrafts. It just brings out the boyish spectacle that makes me giggle."

Boyish spectacle is the best way to put it, and that's what "First Light" really gets right. Yes, the cars and traditional chase scenes are excellent, but what makes this game feel so undeniably Bond are the unexpected moments. We've got the holidays coming up, and you've got a week before GTA VI comes out, so if you haven't played through "007 First Light" yet, there's no better time to do so than the present. Though I guess you've got all the time in the world.

#5707. Trial on Statins for Cirrhosis Won't End Debate Anytime Soon

— Phase III study on simvastatin to prevent hepatic decompensation comes up just short

Statin therapy delivered a statistical near miss at lowering risks of hepatic decompensation and liver cancer in patients with compensated cirrhosis, the phase III SACRED trial showed.

In an intention-to-treat analysis, 8.97% of patients who took simvastatin daily for up to 2 years developed ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage, or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) compared with 18.75% of those who received placebo (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.16-1.05, P=0.064), a difference just short of significant.

Overall survival rates also didn't differ significantly between the statin and placebo groups (HR 2.31, 95% CI 0.24-22.19, P=0.469), reported David Kaplan, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

However, "there is a suggestion that statins may actually reduce decompensation and liver cancer events, but further data will be needed," Kaplan told MedPage Today. What is clear is that statins are safe for patients with cirrhosis and shouldn't be withheld from those who have indications, he added.

"Our hope is that, with additional data from the Liver Cirrhosis Network's RESCU study of rosuvastatin, our data and their data together may be able to move the needle forward on statin initiation," Kaplan said.

Statins could provide anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic benefits while lowering hepatic portal vein pressure in cirrhosis. Observational studies have pointed to lower risks of decompensation and death, including research in veterans with hepatitis C-related compensated cirrhosis and a large study that was also presented at the Liver Meeting in patients with cirrhosis caused primarily by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, randomized trials have shown unfavorable results.

The SACRED trial was conducted at 11 VA medical centers and included patients with high-risk compensated cirrhosis caused by viral hepatitis, alcohol, and/or MASLD. High-risk factors included esophageal varices on endoscopy, portosystemic collaterals on imaging, a vibration-controlled transient elastography liver stiffness of at least 25 kPa, and platelets no greater than 70,000/mm3.

Participants couldn't have a standard indication for statins or statin exposure in the prior 6 months. That exclusion narrowed the study's size and power, Kaplan noted, given the "extremely high fraction" of those in the potentially eligible population who were either on statins or had well-established indications.

Median age was 60 years in the statin group and 64 years in the placebo group. Nearly all patients (93%) were men, and 73.9% were white. Cirrhosis etiology in the statin and placebo groups included alcohol (57.7% and 64.1%, respectively), hepatitis C (39.7% and 37.5%), and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (29.5% and 18.8%). The median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score in both groups was 14. About one-third of both groups were on a non-specific beta blocker (NSBB).

Roughly 40% of the study population had previously cured hepatitis C, Kaplan said, which may have lowered the study's overall event rate and made it more challenging to show a treatment difference.

Of note, HCC occurred in 2.56% of statin patients and 7.81% of placebo patients. HCC events showed the numerically largest difference between the statin and placebo groups, Kaplan noted. Ongoing chemoprevention studies could shed light on how statins might specifically impact liver cancer risk, he added.

The two groups' restricted mean survival times (RMST) showed an advantage with statin therapy. The statin group had an RMST of 702 days compared with the placebo group's 651 days -- a significant 51-day difference (P=0.043). Despite the significance, Kaplan cautioned, "I think one has to be somewhat conservative with the interpretation."

There was also a suggestion of benefit for the primary endpoint when a baseline NSBB was paired with a statin (HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02-1.19, P=0.071).

Adverse event rates were similar in the statin and placebo groups, at 94.9% and 93.8%, respectively. Serious adverse events occurred more frequently in the placebo group (45.3%) than the statin group (35.9%), as did liver-related events (6.3% vs 5.1%). Possible treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 1.6% of the placebo group and 2.6% of the statin group.

Study limitations included the small sample size and the low rates of endpoint events.

#5705. 10 Reasons for the Big Blue Wave

I wrote the other day about a top reason US voters said they voted for Democrats in such large numbers — corruption in the Trump household, Trump administration, and Republican Party. It was surprising to me that this showed up as the biggest factor for so many people … even though it was also a huge one for me. However, I think everyone knows what the most significant reason was for the dramatic, historic shift in voting. It’s the economy, stupid! That’s the famous old quote from James Carville, a political strategist working for Bill Clinton when he was running for president in 1992, and it’s as relevant as ever. With that in mind, let’s take a look at some of the top reasons for the Big Blue Wave.

Inflation has hit and hit and hit. Donald Trump said while campaigning for president in 2024, “Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again.” However, of course, beyond the fact that he didn’t come close to doing that and was just making an obviously false promise, Trump actually jacked up inflation significantly with his obsessive, high tariffs and with his war on Iran. Whereas it’s often hard to tie inflation to a specific presidential policy, in this case, we had two specific presidential policies that clearly caused inflation! Even when there are no clear links, voters blame the president for such matters, so imagine how much they must have done so in this case!

Aside from inflation, the economy overall isn’t great. The country isn’t adding a bunch of jobs, wages and salaries aren’t rising much, and people by and large don’t feel optimistic about their financial futures. So, combined with quickly rising costs, a very meh economy had voters wanting change.

As already discussed at length, voters were fed up with corruption in the Republican Party. As some CleanTechnica readers pointed out, if people were prospering financially and not being hit with severe inflation, many of them probably wouldn’t care about the corruption. However, when considering #1 and #2, people naturally get quite frustrated with blatant corruption and essentially high-volume robbery from Donald Trump, the Trump family, Trump staffers, and the Republican Party broadly.

Naturally, this is heavily linked to #1, since it is largely this war that has led to gas prices rising so much. However, also more broadly, Americans are fed up with forever wars in the Middle East, there’s never been a good and strong case for why Trump started this war (as tends to be the case with these wars in the Middle East), and many people really don’t like seeing innocent schoolchildren being bombed to death. Trump was supposed to be an anti-war president (I know that many people believed that, even though Trump is a naturally aggressive, violent person who seemed to me like someone who would obviously get into wars). Voters who cared a lot about this topic might have felt betrayed by Trump and swung strongly away from him and the Republican Party (which has a tendency to get us into these oil wars in the Middle East).

Even for many people who thought we needed stronger actions to stop people from coming to the United States, the inhumane, deadly, Gestapo-like ICE army — often including violent people with their faces covered and without ID acting like the mafia — was a step or ten too far. There are countless stories of good, innocent people being jailed without cause, or even murdered, by this Nazi-like police force. There was clearly a huge blue shift in certain places as a result of this.

Many voters have gotten extremely concerned about Republicans under Trump’s leadership eroding the foundations of our democracy. While this became a major problem in Trump’s first term, he has gone much further in his second term. Apparently, more people have woken up to this problem and it has freaked them out.

A massive rollout of AI and data centers — often feeling completely forced on us — has upset a lot of Americans. This does come back to #1, too. Giant data centers have jacked up electricity prices a ton in several regions. Others are threatened with the same thing happening. The same thing has also happened from the crypto craze, which more and more people have also found to be a scam. Seeing billions upon billions trillions of dollars funneled toward AI companies while people are struggling, and then seeing electricity prices rising significantly — surprise, surprise — pisses people off and makes them vote for change.

No matter how you cut it, people vote based on money — in particular, their own money. Whether it’s food prices, gas prices, electricity prices, clothing prices, doll prices, computer prices, car prices, or other prices, people don’t like it when they have to pay a lot more money for stuff — especially when they aren’t making much more money, or more money at all. Simply put, this matter deserves extra weight, because the critical thing swing voters are often voting on is just that — money.

Of course, there are solar, wind, and EV aspects to all of this. Trump has made the US spend a fortune to stop wind and solar farms from providing the US with cheap electricity, and he has made the US spend a fortune keeping old, dirty coal power plants open. High gas prices have also pushed people to buy electric cars, but mostly in other countries where there’s more EV choice and more people have more sense on this topic. However, by and large, I don’t think American voters really shifted much based on Trump stopping renewable energy projects, promoting coal and gas, or limiting EV choice in the United States. People voting for Democrats on climate and cleantech matters were already voting for Democrats based on these issues. It’s unlikely many people at all shifted from red to blue because of these factors.
