Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! Today’s stories have me wondering what it must be like to study the human brain: Every new discovery is a breathtaking revelation, and also a reminder of how little we know, and how far the horizon of full understanding still is. It feels a little like looking at the universe, only what is infinite is, in the most literal sense, ourselves.

For many teenagers, phones are pervasive — and destructive. And the policy proposals and scientific research meant to address the crisis are moving too slowly to help a generation already hooked on screens.

But as STAT’s Isabella Cueto reports, a variety of homegrown initiatives are filling the gap, many of them led by teens. Some programs draw inspiration from Alcoholics Anonymous, helping teens develop tools and strategies to refocus and put their devices away. Others are pushing teens to understand the financial incentives behind holding their attention. The techniques are as varied as they are creative: public interventions, manifestos, and overall a movement that is reclaiming attention, real life connections and, ultimately, freedom. Read all about it here.

Biomarker-based diagnostics have improved our understanding of who may develop severe dementia, advancing our knowledge of Alzheimer’s disease and the hope of finding effective early treatment.

Yet for the people who become aware of their heightened risk, the knowledge is bittersweet. The information allows them to act by taking drugs that may delay dementia onset, but it also carries a weight. In a new First Opinion, Neurotransmissions columnist Jason Karlawish shares how learning of elevated risk changed people’s outlook on the future, from bucket lists to plans for care, to considerations about assisted suicide. (And in case you missed it, check out the first installment in this miniseries here.)

The basal ganglia is a gumball-sized region of the brain so central to psychiatric and neurologic conditions that one scientist called it “the Grand Central station of disease.”

Now a massive scientific collaboration has created a map of the area, including a list of which cells are present and how they arranged. This research has led to the discovery of a new type of neuron, and the identification of cells linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Authors consider it a “monumental achievement” that opens the door for understanding the brain in health and disease, but further progress may be at stake amid government funding cuts, Jonathan Wosen reports.

When STAT’s Megan Molteni started investigating the experimental reproductive procedure known as MRT, or mitochondrial replacement techniques, she didn’t know that she would uncover a sprawling international network of clinics that that market to older women.

Over the course of her reporting, she also found evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking. In fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age.

Read more of her takeaways from this eight-month investigation here. And if you haven’t already read Megan’s original investigation, I encourage you to dig in.

Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation brain-computer interface. The Brooklyn-based startup’s device was a wireless version of its first-generation device, which snakes a catheter through veins to park a stent near the brain’s motor cortex. The aim was to connect users to digital devices using brain activity. The pause is not safety related, leaders said.

It’s the first major hiccup for Synchron, one of the leading companies in a fast-growing industry aimed at helping people with disabilities like ALS and paralysis regain independence through brain implants. Synchron will also eliminate jobs in New York City and is working to develop a new device, WIRED reported.

The news gives context to a cryptic comment CEO Tom Oxley gave on a conference panel in New York City last week. “There are hundreds of components in our system, and it just takes a delayed one to slow down your submission to the FDA,” said Oxley, flanked by his competitors at Neuralink and Precision Neuroscience. “We had one particular component that we were caught up on.” – O. Rose Broderick

Come January, Abdul El-Sayed will be the first epidemiologist in the Senate. His election comes as the U.S. is struggling through a spike in measles cases, a Dengue fever outbreak, and a recent foodborne illness crisis.

STAT’s Nick Florko spoke with the senator-elect about how he hopes to rebuild trust in science, as well as who’s responsible for the current state of affairs. “We didn’t have to get here,” El-Sayed said. “In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information-mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame … our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.” Read the whole meaty interview here.

Why ‘brainier’ sports may be better for people with ADHD, The Washington Post

#5646. Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.

Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.

For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.

Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.

"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

#5645. Policy Brief: Trump admin unveils $10B in second-year rural health awards; HHS invests $9.7M to combat elder abuse

Policy Brief: Trump admin unveils $10B in second-year rural health awards; HHS invests $9.7M to combat elder abuse" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this brief. Read below for news from Nov. 2 to 13.

HHS announced a $9.7 million investment Monday through the Administration for Community Living to help prevent elder abuse, neglect and exploitation.

Financial exploitation alone is estimated to cost older Americans $28.3 billion annually, according to the department.

The funding will, among other things, support expanding legal help and strengthening advocacy for those in nursing homes and other care facilities. The ACL will award six new Elder Justice Innovation grants over the next three years, totaling $5.6 million and four new Legal Assistance Enhancement Program grants totaling $1.9 million over two years.

“Older Americans have earned the right to live with dignity, control their own lives, and protect what they worked hard to build,” said Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., HHS secretary, in a statement. “The Trump Administration is investing more than $9.7 million to prevent abuse and financial exploitation, expand access to legal help, and defend the rights of nursing home residents. We are putting practical tools and trusted support into communities to help older Americans safeguard their independence and financial security.”

The Trump administration announced Monday funding for the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), with $10 billion in awards slated for all 50 states.

Similar to fiscal year 2026, Texas and Alaska will receive the largest amount of funding as part of the program. Texas is set to receive $281,976,026, while Alaska will receive $272,653,149.

New Jersey will receive the lowest amount of funding at $142,338,224. Full story.

HHS announced Friday a notice of funding opportunity (NOFO) for its Women’s Initiative for Screening and Health (WISH) program.

The program will award up to $1 million in fiscal year 2027 to establish a multidisciplinary coalition to update HHS’ Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA)-supported Women’s Preventive Services Guidelines.

The funding will fund one organization to create a multidisciplinary panel of at least 10 experts from women’s health, primary care, behavioral health and more. It will also allow the organization to conduct evidence reviews and develop and disseminate information on HRSA guidelines.

“The latest research only makes a difference when it reaches women and the clinicians caring for them,” said Tom Engels, HRSA Administrator, in a statement. “By bringing together clinical expertise and trusted community partners, we can help more women access recommended preventive care nationwide.”

The department says the opportunity advances priorities outlined in an October executive order from President Donald Trump.

CMS plans to trim several “unnecessary” requirements for hospitals and other providers participating in Medicare, including emergency services readiness requirements and staff training for obstetrical services, pushed through during the tail end of the Biden administration.

The proposed rule’s Conditions of Participation (CoP) rollbacks, shared Nov. 5, followed a “comprehensive review” CMS conducted to identify and eliminate “obsolete, outdated and excessively burdensome regulations.” Full story.

CMS finalized its annual outpatient hospital payments rule with a lower-than-proposed rate bump and its major, industry-opposed policy shifts moderated but largely intact.

The 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment Systems rule outlines a 2.3% reimbursement increase for those meeting applicable quality reporting requirements. That’s below the proposed 2.4% increase and reflects a 3.2% projected hospital market basket increase and a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment. Full story.

CMS finalized sweeping Medicare payment reforms it says will shift the program from volume-based "sick care" toward prevention, primary care and accountable care.

The 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule includes a roughly 2% reduction in baseline physician payment rates with targeted increases and new payment opportunities for accountable care, primary and chronic care and behavioral health. Full story.

CMS and HHS announced the finalization of a rule that strengthens oversight of Organ Procurement Organizations (OPO), building on a 2019 Trump executive order.

Key provisions of the final rule include:

“Americans waiting for lifesaving transplants cannot afford poor performance by OPOs, and CMS is committed to holding these organizations accountable,” said Mehmet Oz, M.D., CMS administrator, in a statement. “With today’s new rule, CMS is building on the success of organ procurement reforms from the first Trump Administration to promote clearer documentation, higher donation rates, and swifter consequences for bad actors.”

The Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 25 companies that conduct marketing or generate sales leads for insurers as ACA enrollment season gets underway.

The commission said in an announcement that the letters aim to put these companies on notice about deceptive or unfair marketing tactics that are likely unlawful. Full story.

#5644. Opinion: New organ donation rules are unfair to families

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Tucker is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University.

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.

Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.

Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.

Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.

I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.

The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.

That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.

In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.

These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.

The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.

To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.

Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.

In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.

No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.

I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.

These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.

Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.

First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.

Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.

Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.

The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.

The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.

Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.

In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.

Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

#5643. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

Materials provided by Stanford Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5642. Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire

Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

>Mayo Clinic has announced Matthew R. Callstrom, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, taking over for Gianrico Farrugia, M.D., who in May announced plans to step down at the end of the year.

Callstrom, a radiologist, has been with Mayo Clinic since 2002 who is currently medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy and its AI Program. He's also a member of its board of governors and board of trustees. He's credited for his role in the major nonprofit system's organizational strategy and integration of AI into care.

Farrugia, who has headed Mayo since 2019, plans to stay on through Dec. 31 to ensure a smooth handoff.

>Carl S. Armato, president and CEO of Winston-Salem, North Carolina-based Novant Health, will retire at the end of this year after 15 years leading the system.

Armato joined the nonprofit in 1998 as vice president of finance and operations in its Charlotte and Winston-Salem physician divisions, and held increasing regional and organization-wide leadership roles over subsequent years.

He's credited with boosting access points and unifying Novant's "collection of strong regional organizations into a unified, innovative health system." He also headed substantial growth, with the organization today counting 45,000 employees, 22 hospitals and about 900 total locations.

With his retirement, current Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer John Gizdic will become president and interim CEO on Jan. 1, 2027. His resume includes over 30 years of healthcare leadership, including more than 20 with Novant.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is currently executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo said.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

Parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.

"There are few leaders in healthcare who have the health benefits strategy knowledge and have built the strong relationships that Lisa and James bring to Centivo," said Ashok Subramanian, co-founder and CEO of Centivo, in the announcement. "These new leaders put Centivo in a strong position as we launch in new markets and help more employers across the country tackle rising healthcare costs and restore affordability by rethinking their healthcare benefits strategy."

> Inspira Health CEO Amy Mansue will be retiring at the end of the year, and will be succeeded by current President and Chief Operating Officer Warren Moore, the four-hospital South Jersey system announced this week.

Mansue will have been at the helm for six years, and is credited by the organization for expanding local care access and championing a culture of wellness among its 7,800-person workforce.

Moore has led Inspira's operations since 2021 and was promoted to president at the top of this year. He has 35 years of industry experience and will most immediately prioritize the opening of a new hospital tower and building upon the system's recent Epic launch.

“Leading Inspira has been one of the great privileges of my career,” Mansue said in the announcement. “I’m proud of what our team has accomplished and grateful for the trust of our communities. After working alongside Warren for many years, I know his ability to bring people together, navigate complex challenges and understand what our patients and neighbors count on us to deliver. I have every confidence in his leadership of Inspira’s next chapter.”

> Joint Commission has named Ken Grubbs as its chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1.

Grubbs is the first nurse to serve as COO of Joint Commission Enterprise in organization’s history, according to the Oct. 13 announcement. He currently serves as the organization's chief nursing executive and executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations.

He will succeed James Merlino, M.D., who will take over as the organization's president and CEO this coming January.

> Beth Israel Lahey Health's national leadership search has yielded Peter Shorett as its next president and CEO. His appointment takes effect this coming January.

Shorett is currently the system's senior executive vice president and chief operating officer, and played a role bringing together its Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for an upcoming strategic collaboration for cancer care. Prior to joining in 2019, he was a senior partner at Chartis.

He'll be taking over for Kevin Tabb, M.D., who in March gave notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year. He'd the role at Beth Israel Deaconess since 2011 and guided the organization through its 2019 merger with Lahey Health.

> WellSpan's Board of Directors has named Laureen Driscoll as the Pennsylvania-based system's new president and CEO.

The executive and registered nurse's appointment will go into effect Jan. 4, 2027. She takes over for Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D., who announced plans to retire this past spring.

Driscoll is joining the 12-hospital, $4.7 billion nonprofit from Providence, where she currently serves as chief executive for its south division and oversees 17 hospitals with $10.3 billion of net operating revenue. Prior to that she held roles at MultiCare Health System, Swedish Health System, Le Bonheur Children's Medical Center and Maine Medical Center.

“She has led complex health systems through transformation while strengthening quality, culture, access and performance," Board Chair Joe Crosswhite said in the announcement. "Just as important, she leads with purpose and understands that listening to team members, clinicians and communities is essential. The Board is confident Laureen is the right leader for WellSpan’s next chapter.”

> UnitedHealthcare has elevated Bobby Hunter to the role of president at the insurer.

Hunter wrote in a LinkedIn post that in the new position he will be tasked with leading the charge on the company's modernization efforts, including investments in technology and other initiatives to simplify the healthcare experience for its members.

Hunter most recently served as CEO of Government Programs at UnitedHealthcare, and has held multiple leadership roles at the insurer dating back to 2011.

"The future we're working toward is one where plans and providers work together more seamlessly, information flows instantly, trust is earned through transparency and accountability, and care teams are able to spend more time focused on patients," he wrote in the post. "To get there, we must continue to deliver on the commitments we make to the people, providers, customers, and communities who count on us every day."

> Jonathan B. Perlin, M.D., Ph.D., will retire from his roles as president and CEO of accrediting organization Joint Commission on Dec. 31. Current Chief Operating Officer James I. Merlino, M.D., is slated to succeed him.

Perlin boasted three decades of healthcare executive leadership across his career, which included five at the top of Joint Commission. During that period he oversaw a substantial reduction on Joint Commission standards deemed to be burdensome or obsolete, and programs to support healthcare safety issues in low- and middle-income countries. Titles preceding his time at the organization included president of clinical operations and chief medical officer for HCA Healthcare, and the U.S. Department of Veteran's Affairs' under secretary for health.

Perlin will remain a strategic advisor to the group following his retirement, holding the title of president emeritus.

Merlino's career included leadership roles at Cleveland Clinic such as chief clinical transformation officer and chief experience officer, as well as at healthcare performance improvement company Press Ganey.

> Robert C. Garrett, CEO of Hackensack Meridian Health, will retire next year after decades with the organization, including its formative 2016 merger.

Garrett is set to step down on June 30, upon which time he'll hold the role of CEO emeritus for a year to help ease the transition. The 18-hospital, nearly $10 billion nonprofit said it plans to announce his successor before the year's end.

Garrett began his career in the early 1980s at Hackensack University Medical Center, and in 2009 was named president and CEO of Hackensack University Health Network. When the organization merged with Meridian Health in 2016 to form New Jersey's largest health system, he served as co-CEO for two years before taking on the solo mantle.

Alongside the organization's growth to more than 500 patient care locations, Garrett's tenure also marked the opening of the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, New Jersey's first new medical school in decades.

"Bob has been the driving force behind HMH's unprecedented growth and transformation, its superior quality, innovation and commitment to building an exceptional workforce," Board Chair Keith Banks said in a statement. "At the heart of Bob's legacy is his unwavering belief that we must deliver the most innovative and compassionate care to all patients. HMH is solidly positioned for continued growth, and we are profoundly grateful to Bob and extend our warmest wishes to him for this well-deserved next chapter."

> The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying group for the pharmacy benefit management industry, has named CVS Health executive Ed DeVaney as its board chair.

DeVaney currently serves as president of CVS Caremark, one of the PBM industry's "Big Three" firms. He succeeds Adam Kautzner, president of Express Scripts and Evernorth Health Services, representing one of the other "Big Three" companies.

“The role PBMs play in lowering costs and improving access to prescription drugs for Americans is critically important,” DeVaney said in the announcement. “As Board Chair, I’m committed to ensuring PCMA shares our story with policymakers, consumers and employers so they have a full understanding of the work we do to fulfill our commitment to lower drug costs.”

> UnitedHealth Group has elevated Dan Kueter to serve as the company's chief commercial officer, per a LinkedIn post.

Kueter previously served as the CEO of UnitedHealthcare's commercial business for four years. UHC is the health insurance arm of UnitedHealth Group.

In the new role, Kueter will be tasked with working across both UnitedHealthcare and Optum to support coordination in product development and innovation, he wrote in the post. He said he will also collaborate closely with other senior leaders at the UnitedHealth Group level.

"I'm looking forward to working across the company with colleagues at Optum and UnitedHealthcare to help drive our next chapter of growth and innovation, focused on helping make healthcare work better for everyone," Kueter wrote.

In a separate post, Brandon Cuevas revealed that he will succeed Kueter as CEO of UHC's commercial unit. Cuevas most recently served as executive vice president for the national health plan at Kaiser Permanente, and he previously held multiple leadership roles during a 14-year stint at UnitedHealthcare.

Cuevas said in the post that he "couldn’t be more excited to rejoin a team that is so capable and committed to making positive change in healthcare."

> Optum has named Ujjwal Ratan as the new chief AI officer for its Optum Insight unit, per a LinkedIn post.

In the role, he will be tasked with leading the development of the critical infrastructure that Optum Insight will build its agentic AI toolset on. Ratan has previously held leadership roles at Amazon Web Services and at Oracle, according to his profile.

"Agentic AI only works if the agents have real, connected data to reason over — and few organizations sit across as much of the healthcare journey as Optum does: providers, payers, pharmacy, life sciences and government programs, under one roof," Ratan wrote. "That's exactly the foundation this next wave of AI needs, and exactly why I think Optum is positioned to set the standard for agentic AI across healthcare, not just inside it."

> Association of American Medical Colleges President and CEO David J. Skorton, M.D., will retire from his post on June 30, 2027, the group announced this week. A search for his replacement is currently under way.

Skorton stepped into the role in July 2019 and was kept on by the board in a unanimous 2023 vote. He's credited with guiding the association through the pandemic and overseeing a comprehensive strategic planning process that brought a new vision and mission. Prior to joining he served as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution and was president of Cornell University and the University of Iowa.

“He will be leaving the AAMC an even stronger association than when he arrived," Board Chair Michael Waldrum, M.D., said in a statement. "Identifying a visionary leader to guide the association and the academic medicine community into the future will be our next challenge.”

> Cotiviti, a healthcare infrastructure and data analytics platform, has appointed Erin Schmuker as its chief operating officer.

She enters the role with over 20 years of healthcare leadership, coming directly from a job as president of integrated pharmacies at OptumRx. The new position tasks Schumuker with scaling Cotiviti's operating model, bolstering execution and accountability, simplifying operations and bolstering its growth.

“Our opportunity is to connect data and intelligence to the workflows where decisions are actually made and turn that intelligence into action at scale," President and CEO Ric Sinclair said of the appointment. "Erin is a proven operator who understands how to do that. She knows healthcare, she knows our clients and she knows how to bring people, technology and operations together to deliver results. She will help us move faster, operate better and scale Cotiviti for what healthcare needs next.”

> Kaiser Permanente recently announced that Shaun Smith will be joining as executive vice president and chief people officer, effective Oct. 12.

Smith, who will be reporting directly to the CEO as well as to the president of integrated care and coverage, comes from a chief people and culture officer roles at NewYork-Presbyterian.

> The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) has named Dan Serrano senior vice president and chief financial officer to oversee the organization’s enterprise financial strategy.

Serrano joins BCBSA after holding leadership roles across the health insurance, provider and value-based care sectors. His experience includes serving as chief financial officer for Aetna's Mid-Atlantic Region and holding senior finance positions at ChenMed, Healthfirst, as well as several other home-based and primary care organizations. He also served as vice president of value and risk-based contracting at Mount Sinai Health System.

“Dan's extensive experience across the healthcare ecosystem, combined with a strong track record of aligning financial performance to operational outcomes, makes him a tremendous addition to our leadership team,” said BCBSA president and CEO Kim Keck in a statement.

>Keck Medicine of USC announced that CEO Rodney Hanners will be stepping down on Sept. 24, alongside a handful of other leadership changes at the system and its affiliated Keck School of Medicine of USC.

Hanners was in the role for six years, a period in which he extended the Los Angeles-based organization's reach into Pasadena and the San Gabriel Valley.

Taking over for him will be Steven Shapiro, M.D., currently senior vice president for health affairs, who joined in 2021 from a run as president of the University of Pittsburg Medical Center.

The university noted that it will be trimming the role's responsibilities, reverting supervision of some USC health science schools to the provost "to allow Steve to focus more intensely on elevating our academic medical enterprise."

Beneath him, the university has also named Chief Clinical Officer David Peng, M.D., as deputy executive vice president for health affairs and Keck Medical Center of USC CEO Marty Sargeant as chief operating officer of the broader system. Both Peng and Sargeant will remain in their prior roles alongside the new responsibilities.

USC's announcement also included word that Keck School of Medicine of USC Dean Carolyn Meltzer is stepping down for a new role as president of the Radiological Society of North America. Vassilios Papadopoulos, dean of the university's pharmaceutical school, will be filling her role on an interim basis.

>Health tech company Health Catalyst appointed Simeon Kohl as Chief Executive Officer and President and a member of the company’s Board of Directors, effective September 14.

Kohl most recently served as CEO of Performant Healthcare, a public healthcare company he led through significant strategic and operational transformation, culminating in its sale to Machinify for approximately $670 million. He brings more than 20 years in healthcare, spanning operations, growth and public company leadership. The company’s current CEO and President, Ben Albert, will become Chief Business Officer and will step down from the Board of Directors effective September 13.

During his tenure, Albert led Health Catalyst's strategic priorities and operating initiatives and aligned the leadership team now running the business. He sharpened the company’s focus on its highest-conviction technologies, positioning Health Catalyst as an AI-forward healthcare intelligence company, executives said. To support that focus, he led the divestiture of Vitalware, which enabled the company to retire its approximately $160 million credit facility and strengthen its balance sheet.

> The American Medical Association tapped Jennifer Goldsack as senior vice president and inaugural leader of the AMA Center for Digital Health and AI. Goldsack joins the AMA from the Digital Medicine Society (DiMe), a global non-profit organization dedicated to advancing digital medicine to optimize health, where she was both founder and CEO.

A leading voice on the responsible adoption of digital health and AI in healthcare, Goldsack has a record of bringing together evidence, clinical practice, technology and policy to help ensure digital innovations are safe, effective, equitable and capable of delivering meaningful value for patients and physicians, according to the AMA.

"We are at a defining moment for medicine. Digital health and augmented intelligence are rapidly and fundamentally changing how and where care is delivered. For these tools to reach their full potential and be effective for patients, physicians must lead the way in developing and implementing them. Jennifer is the right leader for this moment because she knows how to bring physicians and innovators together and translate that collaboration into real-world impact on patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., said.

“Reimagining how we care for people in the digital era has been the focus of my career, and we are at an extraordinary moment of opportunity,” Goldsack said in a statement. “We have powerful new tools at our disposal and a responsibility to make sure we harness them to improve people’s lives. I’m thrilled to join the AMA and work alongside physicians and partners across healthcare. We’re going to set a high bar for what better healthcare looks like in the digital and AI era. And together, we will make it happen.”

Since its launch last year, the AMA Center for Digital Health and AI has produced key research, including: a survey of AI usage among physicians, showing growing confidence in the technology’s clinical advantages; and an international survey on wearables.

>Teladoc Health appointed Michael Grasher as its new chief financial officer.

Grasher has more than three decades of experience across the insurance and financial services industries, most recently serving as CFO of property-casualty insurance company IFG Companies, according to an Aug. 31 press release.

"Teladoc Health has built a strong foundation with unmatched scale, deep clinical expertise and a global footprint," said Grasher. "I'm excited to work with Chuck [Divita] and the leadership team to build on that foundation and deliver lasting value for the members, clients and shareholders we serve."

>Johns Hopkins Health Plan has named Daniel Chojnowski as its interim CEO.

Chojnowski has served as the insurer's chief financial officer for the past seven years, according to a post from JHHP on LinkedIn. Former JHHP CEO James Holland departed the organization in mid-August to become president of Medicaid for Humana.

JHHP said in the LinkedIn posted that Chojnowski will "provide stability and trusted guidance" while it conducts a search for a permanent CEO.

"Dan believes in leading with courage and compassion," per the post. "He embodies the modern CFO, which has evolved from the number-crunching budget guard to a strategic partner, helping to steer organizational decisions."

>Wilmington, Delaware-based ChristianaCare welcomed Jenn Schwartz as its new president and CEO on Sept. 1.

The new top exec came to came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer, having previously spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System where she was vice president of legal affairs and general counsel as well as its executive director. She'd already been named as executive vice president and chief strategy officer earlier this year.

Schwartz is taking over for Janice Nevin, M.D., who announced earlier this year she'd be retiring after about 23 years at the nonprofit system. She'd held the top roles for a dozen years.

ChristianaCare is a nonprofit teaching health system with three hospitals hosting 1,430 beds as well as a network of primary care and outpatient services.

Janice Nevin, M.D., will end her 12-year run as president and CEO of ChristianaCare on Sept. 1, the system's board announced.

She retires after 23 years at the organization, initially joining as its chair of family and community medicine. The physician executive is credited by the board with expanding the system's physical footprint, shepherding "significant investment in historically under-resourced areas" and strengthening its academic partnerships.

Taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. She came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer. Prior to that she spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System, where she was vice president of legal affairs & general counsel as well as its executive director.

>Insurer Centene has named Bradley Bolivar as its new chief information officer, with the new role taking effect on Aug. 31.

Bolivar succeeds Brian LeClare, who is set to retire in October. He previously served as CIO at Fannie Mae, where he led strategy around technological development, infrastructure, cybersecurity and more. Bolivar brings more than three decades of technology leadership experience to the role at Centene, according to an announcement from the company.

"We are entering a new era where data, technology and AI are not just business enablers, but strategic capabilities that shape how we operate, innovate and create value," CEO Sarah London said in the announcement. "Brad's proven ability to solve complex technology challenges will position Centene to deliver simpler, better health experiences and improved outcomes for the nation's most underserved populations."

>Elevance Health has named Patrick Fox, M.D., as president of Carelon Behavioral Health.

Fox's background includes more than three decades of experience in clinical psychiatry, behavioral health, public health and health plan leadership, the company said in an announcement. He most recently served as president Elevance-affiliated plan Wellpoint New Jersey.

Fox also previously helmed the company's Colorado Medicaid plan, per the announcement. Fox's new title is effective immediately.

"Patrick brings a rare combination of experience as a practicing psychiatrist, behavioral health leader and health plan executive,” said Kristy Duffey, president of Carelon Health, in the announcement. “He understands the challenges facing behavioral healthcare from the clinical, operational and system perspectives."

"That breadth of experience will be invaluable as we work to improve access, strengthen connections across the healthcare system and deliver better outcomes for the people we serve," said Duffey.

Patrick Gillespie, regional vice president for state affairs at Elevance Health, has been named as Fox's successor as Wellpoint New Jersey president, the company said.

>Providence St. Joseph Health has named a new chief financial officer.

Kevin Smith will take the CFO seat on Oct. 26, according to an announcement from the health system. As CFO, he'll oversee Providence's "inancial strategy, planning, capital allocation and operational performance," the system said.

Smith will join Providence from SSM Health, where he currently serves as CFO. He's also held leadership roles in finance at Luminis Health, Lehigh Valley Health Network, Universal Health Services and the University of Pennsylvania Health System.

“Kevin is a highly respected healthcare finance leader with a strong track record of improving performance, guiding complex organizations and positioning health systems for long-term success,” said Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, in the announcement. “His experience, judgment and commitment to Mission-driven stewardship will be invaluable as we continue strengthening Providence for the future.”

>Accolade executive Shantanu Nundy will join Humana as its new chief medical officer.

Nundy, M.D., currently serves as executive vice president of care delivery and chief health officer at Accolade, a healthcare navigation and care delivery company. He'll step into the role at Humana on Aug. 31, according to an announcement from the company.

Nundy also held leadership roles at Evolent Health, and has provided council to a number of organizations on digital health and AI, including the Food and Drug Administration and World Bank. He continues to practice medicine, including primary care a community health center and hospital-based medicine through a local health system.

Nundy will report to Humana CEO Jim Rechtin as part of the enterprise leadership team.

"Clinical excellence is at the heart of Humana’s vision to be a leading consumer healthcare company, and I am thrilled to welcome Dr. Nundy as our new chief medical officer," Rechtin said in the announcement. "I am confident Shantanu’s experience at the intersection of clinical outcomes, technology and the consumer experience will advance our efforts to simplify the path to care and help the people we serve achieve their best health."

>St. Jude Children's Research Hospital has named Charles W.M. Roberts, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, effective Jan. 1, 2027.

He currently serves as director of the St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center, having joined the organization in 2015 to fill the post. The pediatric hematologist/oncologist has headed the center's five research programs, pushed the center to its best scores in National Cancer Institute rankings and has his own body of medical research that has paved the way to FDA-approved and investigational cancer therapies.

His appointment follows the February announcement from St. Jude that its current leader, James R. Downing, M.D., planned to step down. The organization said it conducted "an extensive international search" before selecting a successor from within.

>CVS Health has announced changes to its board of directors, including the addition of JPMorgan Chase executive Teresa Heitsenrether.

Heitsenrether brings nearly forty years of experience in financial leadership to the board, and currently serves as the chief data and analytics officer at JPMorgan. She will join CVS' board on Nov. 18.

“Teresa’s extensive experience leading complex global businesses and driving technology-enabled transformation will be invaluable as CVS Health continues to innovate on its path to become a consumer focused, health technology company,” CVS CEO David Joyner said in the announcement.

In addition, Larry Robbins has departed CVS' board as of Aug. 13. Robbins has served on the board since 2024, with roles on its Audit and Public Policy and External Affairs Committees.

Robbins is the CEO of Glenview Capital Management.

>Drew Asher, chief financial officer at Centene, will step down from the position in December, the company announced on Monday.

Asher intends to retire from Centene at the end of 2027, per the announcement. He will take the year between stepping down as CFO and retirement to support the transition and ongoing strategic priorities.

Chris Neczypor has been tapped as Asher's successor and will join the company in September, according to the release. Neczypor is a veteran executive who most recently served as CFO at Lincoln Financial, which provides life insurance, annuities and retirement solutions.

He had multiple leadership roles at Lincoln after joining the company in 2018, Centene said. Neczypor spent more than a decade in financial services prior to Lincoln, including a stint as an equity research analyst at Goldman Sachs.

"Chris brings a proven track record of strengthening financial performance, optimizing operations and creating long-term shareholder value," Centene CEO Sarah London said in the announcement. "Just as importantly, he is a collaborative, values-driven leader who understands how to build strong teams and drive meaningful impact."

"Our organization will benefit from his expertise, energy and perspective as we deliver on Centene's next phase of transformation and growth," London said.

Asher has served as CFO at Centene since 2021.

>Humana has named a new executive to lead its growing Medicaid business.

The insurer said Monday that James Holland will join the company as senior vice president and president of Medicaid effective Aug. 17. In the role, he will oversee plans that cover 1.6 million people across 11 states, according to an announcement.

Holland most recently helmed Johns Hopkins Health Plans, overseeing Medicaid, Medicare and other government plans. He has also held leadership roles at Elevance Health, Amerigroup and WellCare Health Plans.

Holland will report to Aaron Martin, president of insurance at Humana.

“Medicaid is an important part of how we deliver on Humana’s purpose, helping some of the most vulnerable populations access the care and support they need to achieve their best health,” Martin said in the announcement. “J.P. brings deep expertise leading government-sponsored healthcare plans and maintaining strong relationships with state and provider partners."

"His experiences and insights will be invaluable as we continue to grow our Medicaid business and better serve our Medicaid members," Martin said.

>Amid the health system's financial strengthening project, Tufts Medicine CEO and CFO have transitioned away from the company.

The current CEO, Mike Dandorph, will step down on September 30, which is also the conclusion of the 2026 fiscal year. He will continue to work towards a transition that ensures Tufts Medicine continues its upward trajectory.

Phil Okala, the COO of Tufts Medicine, will serve as Acting President and CEO. Phil has held multiple leadership roles at Tufts Medicine, and other health systems, including Penn Medicine. With the Board’s full support, he hopes to “focus on guiding Tufts Medicine to greater clinical, operational and financial success.”

Andrew DeVoe, the current Executive Vice President and CFO, has also decided to depart Tufts Medicine, after playing an important role in improving the organization's performance. Soon, Tufts Medicine expects to begin a nationwide search for his replacement. As for right now, Greg Kruse, Tufts’ Vice President of Strategic Operations and Analytics Intelligence, will assume responsibility for future budget planning.

Dandorph said “Serving as President and CEO of Tufts Medicine and working closely with such extraordinary people has been a distinct privilege these past six and a half years. I am proud of what we have accomplished together and am grateful to the amazing physicians, nurses, researchers, learners, staff and leaders whose commitment to our mission has inspired me every day.  I believe this transition is in the best interest and right time for Tufts Medicine. In the coming months, I will work closely with Phil Okala to ensure a thoughtful and orderly transition that best positions the organization for its next chapter and future success.”

>Summa Health announced on August 3 that Jennifer Eslinger will join as the health system's new President and CEO beginning on September 21. She will succeed Daryl Tol, the current Acting CEO, who has led the organization following its acquisition by Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo).

Eslinger brings more than two decades of leadership experience; most recently serving as President and COO of Rochester Regional Health. At Rochester Regional Health, she led the $4.2 billion health system through significant transformation and strategic growth.

"Jennifer is an accomplished healthcare leader with deep experience driving operational and clinical excellence, embracing innovation and creating a culture of curiosity and continuous improvement,” said Kate Walsh, Chair of Summa Health’s Board of Directors. “She has both the judgment and values to build on Summa Health's strong foundation while accelerating our impact in the communities we serve and helping shape the future of healthcare.”

>Jaewon Ryu, the chief executive officer of Risant Health at Kaiser Permanente, has decided to step down from the role to focus on his family. Dale Maxwell, former president and CEO of Presbyterian Healthcare Services, will serve as interim CEO during the national search by the board.

"Jaewon has been instrumental in turning the vision for Risant Health into reality," said Greg Adams, chair and chief executive officer of Kaiser Permanente and chair of the board of Risant Health. "He built an exceptional leadership team, established the organization's operating model, and positioned Risant Health to help more communities benefit from value-based care.”

Ryu served as Risant Health’s inaugural CEO, establishing its operating model and recruiting the initial leadership team. Key moments in his tenure include the addition of both Geisinger and Cone Health as well as meaningful clinical and operational improvements.

The interim CEO, Dale Maxwell, brings over 24 years of executive leadership experience at Presbyterian Healthcare Services, New Mexico's largest nonprofit integrated health system.

"This leadership transition reflects thoughtful planning, not a change in strategy," Adams said.
