#5610. Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Researchers found that using heart scans to guide treatment decisions produced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, even though the scans led to far fewer recommendations to begin taking statins.

The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication. Those advised to use statins based on calcium buildup in their coronary arteries were substantially more likely to follow their treatment recommendations.

Although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment. Researchers say additional studies are needed to determine whether it offers a better strategy for preventing cardiovascular disease.

Why Predicting Heart Disease Risk Remains a Challenge

Cardiovascular disease remains the world's leading cause of illness and death. Much of this burden comes from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which develops when fatty deposits known as plaque accumulate inside arteries, restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke are two major forms of this condition.

Several common factors increase the likelihood of developing ASCVD, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and elevated cholesterol. Doctors use these factors to estimate a person's cardiovascular risk and determine whether preventive medications are appropriate.

Statins are among the most widely used treatments for lowering that risk. These medications reduce cholesterol levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called LDL or bad cholesterol. They also help lower the likelihood of serious cardiovascular complications.

However, identifying which patients stand to benefit from statins remains a significant challenge. Some people who eventually experience a heart attack do not appear to be at particularly high risk under conventional screening methods.

"For far too many patients, the first symptom of ASCVD is a heart attack," said Doctor Joseph B Muhlestein from the Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, USA, the Principal Investigator of the CorCal Outcomes trial. "Statins have been shown to be highly effective in the prevention of ASCVD; however, there is a major gap in risk assessment, statin initiation, and statin persistence."

According to Muhlestein, many people who suffer their first heart attack, particularly younger adults, would not previously have been classified as having enough cardiovascular risk to justify statin treatment. This limitation has prompted researchers to investigate whether directly examining the arteries might provide more useful information.

Can Heart Calcium Scans Improve Statin Decisions?

The CorCal Outcomes trial investigated two different approaches for determining which patients should be advised to begin statin therapy before experiencing a cardiovascular event.

The first relied on the pooled cohort equations (PCE), a commonly used risk assessment tool that estimates cardiovascular risk using traditional factors such as age, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and smoking status.

The second approach measured coronary artery calcium (CAC), which provides a more direct indication of plaque buildup in the arteries supplying the heart.

This measurement uses a computed tomography (CT) scan to detect calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can accumulate within atherosclerotic plaque, making it a useful marker of underlying coronary artery disease, even in people who have not developed symptoms.

Unlike traditional risk calculators, which estimate the likelihood of future cardiovascular problems based on personal characteristics and health measurements, calcium scans provide evidence of disease already present in the coronary arteries.

Researchers wanted to determine whether using this information to guide statin recommendations could improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Nearly 5,800 Patients Put Both Methods to the Test

The trial enrolled 5,772 patients from the Canyons and Desert regions of Intermountain Health Care in the United States. Participants had no known history of ASCVD or diabetes and had not previously received statin therapy.

Their average age was 64, and women accounted for 51% of the study population.

Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to one of two groups. One group received statin treatment guidance based on traditional cardiovascular risk scores, while the other received recommendations based on coronary calcium scan results.

Both patients and their physicians were informed of the treatment recommendations generated by the study protocol. However, the final decision about whether to start taking statins remained with the patients and their doctors.

The researchers then tracked major cardiovascular events (MACE; all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and arterial revascularization).

This combined outcome included death from any cause, heart attacks, strokes, and procedures to restore blood flow through narrowed or blocked arteries.

Heart Scans Led to Far Fewer Statin Recommendations

After an average follow-up of 4.2 years, researchers found that major cardiovascular events occurred at exactly the same observed rate in both groups.

A total of 2.7% of patients in each group experienced one of the events included in the study's primary outcome. The estimated relative risk over time was also nearly identical (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% confidence interval 0.71 to 1.38; p=0.045 for noninferiority).

However, this similarity did not establish that the two strategies were equally effective. The study failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement for demonstrating that the calcium scan approach was not meaningfully worse than conventional risk assessment.

A notable difference emerged in how frequently patients were advised to begin taking statins.

Participants evaluated using traditional risk scores received recommendations to start statin therapy more than three times as often as those whose decisions were guided by coronary calcium measurements.

Despite this substantial difference in treatment recommendations, both groups experienced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events during the follow-up period.

A Surprising Difference in Statin Adherence

Perhaps the most intriguing finding involved whether patients actually followed their prescribed treatment.

Among those advised to take statins, patients whose recommendations were based on calcium scans were much more likely to adhere to their medication regimen than those assessed using traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

The difference was substantial (62% vs. 23%).

In other words, patients recommended statins based on visible evidence of calcium buildup in their arteries were approximately 2.7 times as likely to follow their medication regimen.

One possible explanation is that seeing evidence of disease in their own arteries makes patients more motivated to take preventive medication. However, the trial did not establish why adherence differed so dramatically between the groups.

The findings raise the possibility that coronary calcium scans could influence not only which patients receive statin recommendations, but also whether those patients consistently take the medications.

What the Findings Mean for Heart Disease Prevention

Despite these potentially important differences, the researchers emphasized that the study could not establish whether calcium scan-guided treatment provides cardiovascular protection comparable to traditional risk assessment.

One important limitation was that fewer participants experienced major cardiovascular events than the investigators had anticipated. With fewer events to analyze, the trial had less statistical power to determine whether a meaningful difference existed between the two approaches.

"The power of the study to detect a difference was reduced by the lower-than-expected event rates and we did not demonstrate noninferiority between the groups," said Doctor Muhlestein, who concluded: "The study did provide important hypothesis-generating insights into the efficiency of statin initiation and adherence when decisions are based on CAC scoring. Taken together, our data could be used to plan an additional well-powered randomized trial comparing CAC with current risk factor-based algorithms."

The findings may help researchers design future trials capable of determining whether coronary calcium scans can improve the efficiency of statin prescribing without compromising cardiovascular protection.

Current European recommendations already recognize a potential role for these measurements. The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidemias recommends considering increased coronary calcium scores, when available, as an additional factor in cardiovascular risk assessment.

This guidance applies particularly to people at moderate cardiovascular risk or those whose estimated risk falls near the threshold at which preventive medication would normally be recommended.

For these individuals, evidence of calcium buildup may help doctors make more informed decisions when the need for statin therapy is uncertain.

The CorCal Outcomes findings add to the discussion by suggesting that heart scans may also influence how faithfully patients follow treatment. Whether that advantage translates into better long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains an important question for future research.

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5609. Joanna Gaines Reveals How Her Approach to Holiday Decorating Has Evolved as She’s Gotten Older

Joanna Gaines keeps a beautifully decorated home year-round, so it’s no surprise that she pulls out all the stops for the holidays.

The “Fixer Upper” star recently shared her best holiday hosting tips as she prepares to celebrate the season with her family. She also noted the surprising way her approach has changed over time.

“The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” Gaines, 48, told USA Today. “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.”

While the Magnolia co-founder encouraged aspiring decorators to feel empowered to go big with their festive displays, she left room for those who prefer to take a more subdued route.

“There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.”

Gaines also noted that she’s committed to upholding food traditions, using recipes she’s been working on since she and Chip Gaines wed in 2003.

“Food is really at the center of our holidays,” she said. “Thanksgiving especially is this day I feel like I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.”

Gaines also detailed her approach to Christmas in the editor’s note she published in the Nov. 10 issue of Magnolia Journal.

“Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.”

She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory.

“Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.”

Explaining that she’s choosing to prioritize holding space for both the major moments and the much more relatable ones, Gaines also reflected on being the “gatekeeper” of her family’s yearly traditions as she aims to “do the same things” they always have, “if not bigger and better” this year.

She wrote about the “dressing up” that is encouraged toward the end of the year and romanticized the “fresh delight” of decorating the home, hosting loved ones, and “trying to create standout experiences” that her “kids will remember and tell their kids about someday.”

The Gaineses certainly have their hands full with their five children: Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8. But during a recent conversation on the “Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce” podcast, the proud mom revealed that they’d recently been discussing the idea of expanding the family once again.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

“He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” Gaines quipped, adding that her husband had even told their “grown kids” that she was expecting, and their eldest daughter said that she’s “not coming home” if the news is true.

The HGTV personality went on to encourage Kelce, a mom of four, to add another little one to her family.

“Five is a good number,” Gaines said, noting that she would “have more babies” if she “could.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5607. Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

A new national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal important clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction. While smoking remains the most popular method among US adults who use cannabis, roughly one in seven consumes it in nearly every available form. Researchers found that this group had particularly high rates of daily use and cannabis use disorder.

Cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor. Its use is widespread in the United States. Recent national survey figures indicate that approximately 43.8 million Americans ages 12 and older (more than 15 percent) had consumed cannabis within the previous 30 days.

Researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption. Nearly half of users, 48 percent, primarily smoked cannabis, while 21 percent combined smoking and vaping. Another 17 percent mainly consumed edibles. The remaining 14 percent belonged to what researchers called the "polymodal group," meaning they used cannabis in almost every available form.

Cannabis Addiction Rates Differ Sharply by Consumption Pattern

The findings, published online August 8 in the journal Addictive Behaviors, revealed major differences in how frequently these groups consumed cannabis. Approximately half of people in the polymodal group reported using it every day. Daily use was considerably less common among other participants, occurring in 28 percent of those who primarily smoked, 31 percent of those who smoked and vaped, and about 13 percent of those who mainly consumed edibles.

An even more striking difference emerged when researchers examined cannabis use disorder, the medical diagnosis associated with cannabis addiction. About 67 percent of polymodal users met the criteria for the disorder, compared with 47 percent of those who both smoked and vaped, 36 percent of those who mainly smoked, and just 15 percent of participants who primarily used edibles.

"Our findings suggest that using cannabis in multiple forms may be a red flag for heavier use and symptoms of addiction," said study lead author Omar El-Shahawy, MD, PhD, MPH, an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. "Asking patients not only whether but how they use cannabis could help clinicians identify when a fuller assessment may be warranted."

To investigate these patterns, the research team examined responses from 17,732 adults who had used cannabis during the preceding month. The information came from the 2022-2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Using statistical methods to identify similarities in participants' consumption habits, the researchers conducted the first national analysis of how different methods of cannabis use naturally group together.

Younger Adults More Likely to Use Multiple Forms of Cannabis

The researchers also discovered notable differences in the characteristics of people who preferred particular consumption methods. Young adults ages 18 to 25 accounted for nearly one-third of both the smoking and vaping group and the polymodal group. In contrast, only about one sixth of participants who primarily smoked cannabis belonged to that age range.

Edibles showed a different demographic pattern. Women made up more than half of those who mainly consumed edible cannabis products, and this method was particularly common among college graduates. However, the study did not investigate what motivated participants to choose specific consumption methods, leaving the reasons for these differences unresolved, according to Dr. El-Shahawy.

Another finding raised concerns about the potential effects of inhaling smoke. People who smoked cannabis were more likely to also smoke cigarettes than those who mainly vaped cannabis or consumed edibles. Because both tobacco and cannabis smoking involve combustion (burning), people who regularly smoke both substances may expose their lungs to additional harmful chemicals.

"The strong tie between smoking cannabis and smoking cigarettes is of concern because this subset of people are breathing in a wider range of chemicals via combustion, and their lungs are at risk," said senior author Joseph J. Palamar, PhD, MPH, a professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Why Cannabis Prevention Messages May Need to Change

The findings suggest that health education should account for the different ways people consume cannabis rather than concentrating primarily on smoking. Different consumption patterns may call for different approaches to explaining potential risks, particularly among younger adults and people who regularly combine several methods.

"Public health messages about cannabis still focus mostly on smoking, but people now use the drug in many different ways," said Dr. El-Shahawy. "For younger adults, that means talking about the risks of vaping and combining multiple forms, while for people who prefer edibles, the message is to 'start low and go slow' because the effects take time to kick in."

The researchers hope to investigate the motivations behind these consumption patterns in future work. According to Dr. El-Shahawy, one question is whether people who favor edibles are more likely to use cannabis to manage problems such as pain or difficulty sleeping.

The team also emphasized several limitations. Because participants described their own cannabis habits, some may not have reported their consumption accurately or completely. The observational study also cannot determine whether using multiple forms of cannabis directly increases addiction risk. It establishes an association between consumption patterns and cannabis use disorder, rather than proving that one causes the other.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health through grant R01DA055675.

Additional NYU Langone researchers who contributed to the study included Mohsen Abbasi-Kangevari, MD, MPH; Michelle He; and Xiaoying Zheng, alongside Drs. El-Shahawy and Palamar. Neal Doran, PhD, of the University of California, San Diego, also served as a study co-investigator.

Materials provided by NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5606. DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues

A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium during a shooting spree on Thursday, police said.

The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area.

Matt Wade Lambert, 55, a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life.

Lambert was suspected of going down to the luxury VIDA Fitness center housed inside the building, locating the building manager, identified las 46-year-old James Stuart, next to the treadmills and shooting him with a handgun from a point-blank range, DC Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, according to WUSA9.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gymgoer James Spellman told The Associated Press. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout in the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and an order to shelter in place in the area.

While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect.

During a press conference Thursday evening, Interim DC Police Chief Jeff Carroll said that Lambert then ran out of the gym, went up to his seventh-floor patio and opened fire from a rifle, striking two men and two women who were downstairs. Earlier reports said three of them were construction workers.

One of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he ended his own life with a shotgun blast.

When officers breached the door, they found all three firearms used during the shootings, along with containers of flammable liquid.

DC Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence."

Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025. In it he claimed that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage.

Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment.

According to the filing, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027.

Attorney Joel Braithewaite, who represented Lambert in the case, told NBC News that he spoke with him just yesterday or the day before and said that the 55-year-old was "in a good place" and about to start a new job on Monday.

#5604. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5601. Nearly Half of Gen Z Admit Skipping Rent or Mortgages Just To Fund Holiday Spending

The holiday season is an exciting time, but it can also be very expensive.

If you’re careless, festive gatherings, gifts, and travel may leave you in debt well into the new year.

A new survey by Accredited Debt Relief found that 67% of Gen Z have taken on or expect to take on holiday debt this year. And nearly 15% of Americans are still paying off last year’s holiday debt.

Furthermore, 46% of Gen Z respondents have delayed or skipped rent or mortgage payments to afford holiday spending, compared with 28% of millennials, 14% of Gen X, and 3% of baby boomers.

“Holiday spending should never come at the expense of someone's financial stability, but these findings show just how difficult it can be to balance financial responsibilities with the social expectations and pressure to create a memorable holiday," said Bobbi Rebell, chief financial education adviser at Accredited Debt Relief in San Diego.

"Making tough choices around spending may feel like you’re disappointing those you care about, but protecting your financial future needs to be non-negotiable."

If you’re worried about holiday debt or keeping up with housing expenses, a bit of planning, dedication, and creativity can help you enjoy the season without putting your finances on the line.

Experts agree that your rent or mortgage and related bills should always come first, before you spend money on holiday extras.

“I’ve spent a lot of time helping people who have struggled to keep their homes. And I’ve seen how hard it can be to recover once things get out of control and they start falling behind on mortgage payments,” says Casey Yontz, bankruptcy attorney at Yontz Law, PLLC in Phoenix.

One missed mortgage payment probably isn’t going to get you into foreclosure, but it can be the beginning of a snowball of serious delinquency.

And depending on the terms of your loan, you can incur late fees on your missed payment.

Once that payment is 30 days late, it could get reported to credit bureaus and take a serious toll on your credit score. If you continue to fall behind, foreclosure is a possibility.

“It’s true that under federal mortgage-servicing rules, foreclosure generally cannot begin until you are 120 days behind. But this doesn’t mean you should treat these 120 days as extra time to spend money on something else, like holiday gifts or travel,” Yontz explains.

According to Yontz, there’s no holiday present that’s worth putting your family's home at risk.

Howard Dvorkin, chairman at Debt.com in Fort Lauderdale, FL, shares those thoughts.

“What’s worse: Someone thinking you cheaped out on their holiday gift? Or sleeping outside? Financially speaking, housing must be your top priority. I’ve yet to meet a client’s friends and family who would want you to jeopardize your housing,” says Dvorkin.

If you're still paying for the 2025 holidays, putting 2026 holiday expenses on another credit card is not the solution.

“Holiday debt is an indicator that your holiday spending is beyond your budget, and might be a little bit out of control,” says Yontz.

Stop adding to it, and be honest with yourself about the math.

Look at your actual income versus expenses and debt numbers.

Ask yourself these questions: How much do I still owe? What’s the interest rate? How much can I afford to pay each month after paying my living expenses?

“Try to prioritize higher-interest card debt first. Pay more than the minimum payments, because making minimum payments on credit cards is like throwing buckets of water on a five-alarm fire,” say Yontz.

Dvorkin also recommends seeking professional help.

“Call a certified credit counselor and receive a free, in-depth debt analysis. With that in hand, you can consider all your options and make an informed choice,” explains Dvorkin.

Depending on your situation, a debt management program may make sense. It can reduce your total credit card payments by up to half without any long-term damage to your credit score.

“It can also lower your interest rate to 10% or less—sometimes even zero. You pay a fee for a professional to set this up, but those fees are dwarfed by how much you save,” Dvorkin adds.

Holiday spending should come out of whatever disposable income you have left after paying for your necessities like housing, gas, and groceries.

These tips can help you enjoy the holiday season while still keeping your finances in check:

You'll save more if you focus on what to buy than how you buy it. That’s why a holiday budget is so important.

“Nothing evokes images of Scrooge more than sitting down with pen and paper and listing everything you'll buy. But we don't live in 'A Christmas Carol.' We have the technology to make holiday budgeting a breeze. There’s no shortage of apps that act as busy little elves and do the work for you,” say Dvorkin.

Inviting family members over for a no-cost game night will be far more memorable than buying each of them a shiny, new gadget.

“I just lost my mom this spring, and I can guarantee you that no present could ever be better than more time with her. Presents don’t matter, people do, in my opinion," Yontz explains.

You’ll notice a lot of companies that will let you buy something for the holidays and pay for it over time, especially if you’re shopping online.

Unfortunately, they’re not making your purchase any cheaper. In fact, you will probably end up paying more with interest and fees.

“They tempt you, and you pay for it. Don’t fall down the buy now, pay later chimney of misfit payments,” says Yontz.

Train your brain to dislike overspending.

Do some research on how much you’re actually paying for credit card debt if you have it. Notice how much you’re paying in interest when you buy something.

“When I started doing this, I felt like I was being taken advantage of and that was enough for me to not want to use credit cards,” Yontz explains.

At the end of the day, the holidays should be something your family remembers fondly, not something you're still paying for next Christmas.

#5599. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

“I did watch the Lamar documentary. I’m not too thrilled about it,” she said.

“I’m watching the documentary, and I’m like, 'Wait, I took time out of my life to sit here and do a favor for you,'” she continued on the family’s reality show. “I’m not being paid. I’m doing this ‘cause I’m trying to be nice.”

Kardashian found “many things” Odom said in the documentary to be “really distasteful.”

After the split, it was reported that Kardashian kept the couple’s marital mansion, which was located in an upscale guard-gated community called Mulholland Estates in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Tarzana.

The former couple purchased the home for $3.95 million in December 2009, about two months after their wedding day.

#5597. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5596. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5595. IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry

SPECIAL BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

QDC26 shows progress in the hardware, software and tooling around quantum computing as customers look for evidence of better outcomes.

IBM Corp.’s Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week marked a change in emphasis. IBM claims that researchers have demonstrated quantum advantage in 2026 by working with the classical computing community. Its public presentations showed progress in processors, error correction, scientific software and the integration of quantum with conventional computing.

The company’s quantum leader, Jay Gambetta (pictured), also set a new target. The next big milestone comes by demonstrating industry impact by 2028, conditional on collaboration across enterprise application researchers and the classical and quantum communities.

Our key takeaway is that IBM is assembling more of the full system required to turn a quantum experiment into useful scientific work. Hardware is important, but the real innovation will come from software. Importantly, the tools that help a scientist formulate a problem, run it across different computing resources, check the result and understand the economics are where much of the innovation is headed. These capabilities address several of the barriers customers described to us in our spring quantum tour of major scientific research labs; and the issues discussed with technologists on our Quantum 101 Series at theCUBE’s NYSE studio.

Despite the progress being made, the remaining gaps and challenges are many. Quantum science is advancing but impact on industries is still years away. Better software is the key to making dramatic improvements in quantum performance and a new service capability can attract researchers. But if a chemist needs to understand the deep nuances of quantum computing, it limits adoption. We believe the next phase of innovation will focus on abstracting quantum complexities and making measurable improvements in simplicity to drive further usage.

In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine IBM’s public QDC proclamations through the prism of our spring interviews with six quantum and supercomputing experts. We add customer perspectives from our partner Qualitate, assess the implications of IBM’s foundry investments and consider what evidence would signal that progress is moving from scientific advantage to industry impact.

IBM’s progress comes into better focus when evaluating its milestones separately. IBM’s goal of demonstrating Quantum Advantage by 2026 is generally accepted as met, based on achieving particular computation superiority relative to today’s classical methods. But to truly show industry impact, IBM needs to show results make a difference to an organization. Milestones around fault-tolerant architectures will increasingly focus on the ability to sustain reliable computation in the face of errors. Progress in one category will definitely support another but it’s useful to look at milestones and proof points separately as shown below.

IBM deserves high marks for achieving that advantage but is subject to scrutiny. Gambetta’s keynote described classical researchers overtaking quantum results, claims being withdrawn as classical makes improvements, and subsequent quantum work moving the needle in favor of quantum again. This of course is how a competitive scientific ecosystem should operate. We’re eager to see the leapfrogging end and await a day where a quantum advantage becomes sustainable with clear evidence that classical computing has no chance of catching up for specified use cases.

Observers can rightly be concerned that incorrect inferences may be drawn from the term “advantage.” The phrase can sound like a statement of superiority. But if that advantage is not consistently held, then the broader industry might remain skeptical. The same applies to verifying that a customer outcome is attributable an underlying scientific model powered by quantum.

A public Allstate example is useful and illustrates the difference. IBM described underwriting-optimization results as comparable to classical optimization schemes. That can represent progress, but it does not show that quantum has delivered a superior underwriting outcome. Customers need to decide how much they are prepared to invest in learning before a measurable benefit appears. IBM, in our view, is working hard to simplify the heavy lift and broaden adoption.

The researchers we interviewed in spring 2026 for World Quantum Day were already thinking beyond the hardware. Their concerns included application selection, reliability, integration, software complexity and the ability to preserve optionality as hardware evolves. These were six independent editorial interviews conducted on theCUBE, made possible by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., across five institutions, offering a view of the work required to make quantum useful. The discussions were hosted by this author and Paul Gillin, managing editor at SiliconANGLE.

The following table highlights the to priority stated by each researcher at the time and our take on how IBM has responded in the past 6-9 months.

IBM is directing effort toward problems that these practitioners identified months earlier. We believe that is a strong indicator of product relevance, an even more important than hardware milestones.

It also gives us a more reasonable test of true progress. A scientist must be able to attack a meaningful problem with less setup effort, run it more reliably and compare the result with a credible classical alternative. IBM’s public announcements show capabilities intended to support that progression and the gaps identified this spring by our researcher friends. Thus far, however, they don’t show how broadly researchers can complete their tasks without specialist assistance. IBM shared additional capabilities to a small group of industry analysts under NDA, which look encouraging.

Some of the most interesting material in Chicago concerned ordinary operational friction. In the public developer sessions, IBM described experiments interrupted by sleeping laptops, dead notebook sessions, running out of memory or tokens, and lost work in process. In quantum research, as with AI YOLO training runs, they add expense and blockers to work that already requires specialized expertise.

Managed workflows address this through simplification by moving execution into a hosted environment with conventional computing resources and tools to capture and save work in process. Researchers can associate quantum jobs with the workflow and monitor consumption across both quantum and classical support infrastructure. That creates a basis for repeating experiments and understanding where resources are consumed and how to optimize the complete process.

Take the chemistry approaches discussed at the event. Researchers can divide a larger molecular problem into smaller parts, use quantum or classical computing methods for appropriate parts and combine the results. At QDC26, IBM described improvements in classical algorithms that support the processing of quantum jobs. Classical solving steps can become a major bottlenecks and represent opportunities for optimization.

The relevant focus is increasingly the complete research workflow. Here we’re referring to the preparation, the quantum work, the classical processing and the validation. This expands the opportunity for IBM and its partners because more of the work can be supported through its software and services. It also shines a light on how the economic case needs to evolve, with a focus on the cost of an outcome.

Faster quantum hardware alone is not the answer. Conversely, better classical software can make quantum experiments much more productive. Both are developments that came into focus at QDC26. Customers need enough visibility to identify the bottlenecks and implement improvements.

IBM’s pronouncements about AI are expected to address barriers raised in our spring interviews – the complexity of translating domain knowledge into a working quantum experiment. IBM must provide skills that assist with choosing methods, workflows, applying classical algorithms and the like. And validating implementations before longer, more expensive runs take place. Our developer conversations at the event underscore demand for AI assistance with calls for simpler packaging and managed services.

We believe this marks is an important near-term relationship between AI and quantum. AI can help scientists use quantum computing more effectively before quantum delivers a broadly demonstrated improvement in AI itself. The immediate opportunity is to simplify – reducing the effort required to apply specialized software and infrastructure.

This requirement has implications for how scientific software is packaged. A library contains reusable code. Increasingly, skills will supply context and guidelines for selecting and applying that code. As skills improve, we expect more of the integration work to be assisted by software. The value of a mature library will still depend on its performance and suitability for the task at hand. The public QDC releases include libraries, mapping tools and AI skills together; they hint toward an evolution in how software will be used in the future.

Another gap is accountability. For example, what happens if a workflow executes but uses invalid scientific assumptions. An AI-generated configuration can appear valid while making a poor trade-off between accuracy and cost, for example. In our view, a useful abstraction must maintain the ability to understand those AI decisions and validate them in terms that a domain expert/scientist comprehends.

This is where customer evidence must become more specific in our view. For example, can a chemist repeat useful work without a vendor team guiding them every step? Can another scientist reproduce the result? Can the organization see what exactly changed between runs? We would place considerable weight on those conditions when judging whether easier programming translates into broader scientific adoption.

Chemistry and materials are fields that provide a strong connection between our spring interviews and the public QDC discussions. Johansson at CSC emphasized the challenge of modeling interacting electrons. Beck at Oak Ridge described materials and chemistry research with potential relevance to fusion and biology. IBM’s sessions discussed tools for decomposing problems and processing results across quantum and conventional systems working in tandem.

We view these fields as particularly credible places to look for early useful applications because the scientific problems involve quantum behavior. That is a reason to prioritize research that benefits from quantum. Problem scope, accuracy and economics (or feasibility) relative to conventional methods will determine the ultimate usefulness of quantum.

IBM’s performance progress is notable, but its points of comparison are instructive. Its headline 25-fold improvement in maximum circuit throughput compares Nighthawk r2 with Heron. Several application improvements also compare newer IBM quantum systems with earlier ones. Those figures demonstrate progress within IBM’s generations but a customer still needs a comparison with the best practical classical approach to the same problem.

The mot useful metric in our view is the cost and time required to obtain a validated outcome. The calculation should include all aspects of conventional preprocessing and post-processing, the quantum work done, job completion times and the intensity of the technical skills required perform and validate the result. Importantly, an important future measure is whether the process can be consistently repeated at scale.

Customers should absolutely invest before quantum consistently wins. The key is to identify those investments as a learning experience.

Post-quantum cryptography or PQC is a topic we unpacked at theCUBE’s Quantum Readiness Day this past September. Qualitate customer survey findings add another dimension to our PQC analysis. But don’t confuse PQC spend with quantum application adoption.

A query of Qualitate’s interview data on quantum adoption focuses heavily on PQC, a tactical topic that is top of mind for enterprises today. Organizations are spending to prepare existing information systems to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. The data include customers already taking action, as well as those evaluating.

“Now is the time we’re really starting to go all in on post quantum cryptography.”

The same participant, a technology lead at a professional services company, explains the rationale in terms of future loss avoidance:

“We anticipate that this will significantly save us on dealing with enormous crises in the future.”

Today’s enterprise focus as it relates to quantum is on modernizing cryptography. This is far ahead of investing to find useful applications for a quantum computer. Today’s practitioners are consumed with deploying and securing agents and making AI trustworthy. Quantum applications, other than PQC, are not top-of-mind for most enterprise customers. Security work to protect conventional systems is tactical and there’s little evidence of interest in running workloads on quantum hardware within organizations today.

NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024 and encourages organizations to begin transitioning. Its guidance also explains the risk that adversaries collect encrypted information today for possible decryption later. Unlike Y2K, which had a definitive date associated wth the risk, the timing of a capable quantum attack remains uncertain. As such, migration planning is sensible now, independent of IBM’s application and hardware milestones.

The following competitive signals are seen in the Qualitate data and are almost exclusively security-related:

The opportunity for specialists also remains open. One participant states:

“The field is still not crystallized. And probably we will not necessarily rely on the hyperscalers. Probably will rely on specialists.” – Global head of analytics, financial services and insurance, large U.S. corporation (Source: Qualitate)

Our take is that technical credibility and existing relationships, combined with the ability to affect a successful migration, may all influence these purchases. IBM has many assets, but customers are still evaluating alternatives. Success in quantum-safe security strengthens its commercial position without, by itself, resolving which quantum computing architecture or application platform will prevail when quantum goes mainstream.

Quantum computing also needs to progress from building exceptional devices to producing dependable systems repeatedly. The manufacturing announcements around IBM’s roadmap deserve scrutiny in that context.

In September, IBM acquired, Anderon, finalizing a $1 billion CHIPS award supported by an additional $1 billion IBM investment. IBM has reported it has an Albany, New York-based, 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry serving customers across the ecosystem, with initial wafers already running through the facility.

Our view is that the learning curve will be as important as any single milestone. More repeatable production can confer experience advantages to IBM (Wright’s Law), much in the same way Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has demonstrated its leadership in semiconductor manufacturing. Serving multiple customers could help support volume across shared infrastructure. Whether those benefits emerge depends on demand, process stability, yields and the ability to protect each customer’s intellectual property. In addition, IBM can learn from Intel’s missteps and its own foundry challenges.

The industry needs to watch for manufacturing progress alongside qubit performance. Capital investments are followed by innovation. IBM’s August acquisition of HRL Laboratories adds a related strategic chess move. The rationale explained by IBM is to acquire expertise in silicon-spin qubits, sensing, materials, cryogenics, controls, packaging and interconnects. IBM describes that expertise as complementary to its superconducting work and identifies opportunities to collaborate with Anderon.

We interpret the acquisition as a way for IBM to control its destiny in a return to its vertically integrated mainframe past. At the same time, it doesn’t have the volume economics to achieve its objectives purely as a captive/integrated systems player. So it must open up its manufacturing capability to other parties, including its competitors.

Taken together, the public announcements at QDC26 suggest a broader platform ambition. IBM is connecting access to quantum hardware and software with classical computing, application functions, development tools and the like. We believe this could increase its role in the customer’s research process and create more opportunities for ecosystem partners to package specialized capabilities.

The competitive advantage will come from making useful work easier to perform and repeat. A customer that can move from a scientific experiment to a reliable result at scale, with less effort, has a reason to stay with a vendor and invest more. That advantage still has to be earned through application quality, performance, service reliability and superior economics.

There is also a customer tradeoff – the classic lock-in risk. An integrated service can reduce operational complexity while increasing dependence on the provider’s tooling and ecosystem. Open-source tools help minimize the risk, but portability also depends on whether models, workflows, validation and operational models transfer to another platform. Our spring conversations with Kranzlmüller – and his emphasis on technological independence – along with Shehata’s interest in interoperable specifications – make that point clear.

We would not declare IBM as a decisive winner from this conference. But the company has presented an impressive combination of hardware, software and infrastructure progress. Customers will determine its value through repeated use and outcomes. Competing systems from specialists and hyperscalers – as well as progress from classical methods – will continue to shape the narrative.

If Jay Gambetta’s prediction holds true, the next two years will produce a more tangible conversation around industry impact. Look for significantly more quantum POCs, more named customers solving consequential problems and a measurable change in a scientific or business decision. We would also want enough evidence for an independent team to assess the contribution; and for the customer to explain the full cost of achieving an outcome.

For enterprise leaders, the sensible approach is to separate cryptographic readiness from quantum application programs tied to specific problems and economics.

IBM has made a stronger case that the surrounding machinery for useful quantum computing is coming together. The future test is whether customers can show what changed because of quantum. A demonstrably improved scientific result or an economically superior workflow would make the 2028 ambition impressive.

That is the evidence we will be watching.

What’s on your quantum radar? Let us know.

#5594. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5592. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

Buyers rarely get low rates and strong negotiating power at the same time, and today’s market is handing you the leverage. Connect with a local real estate agent to find homes where sellers may be open to covering a rate buydown or closing costs, so you can see if today’s market can work for your budget.

#5591. October Existing-Home Sales Sink to 16-Year Low; Rates Only Partly to Blame

The National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) Existing-Home Sales report for October came in on a somewhat dismal note: Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month to a rate of 3.75 million.

That marks the lowest level since August 2010’s 3.68 million, according to Realtor.com®  Chief Economist Danielle Hale.

Year-over-year home sales were down 8.8% compared to October 2025, which recorded a sales pace of 4.11 million.

Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West, but held steady in the relatively “inventory-constrained” and “competitive” Northeast market, Hale noted. Year-over-year sales, however, declined for all four regions.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun blamed mortgage rates. “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” he said.

As the housing market enters its slowest season, rates that have held above 7%—a huge leap from before the Iran War, when they touched 6%—have depressed demand and discouraged many buyers, who already face longer-term issues with housing affordability.

Hale concurred with Yun’s diagnosis. According to her, climbing mortgage rates in September (the time when many October closed sales would have been in contract) “were the highest rates of 2026 at the time…and they likely derailed some homebuying plans.”

If mortgage rates “derailed” home-buying plans in October, could the recent ease in mortgage rates signal a gentler turn in the market in the coming months?

Hale thinks the story is not so simple. In her words, the October market “reflect(ed) a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

She added that “several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go, including a strong economy and jobs market, persistent inflation, and an expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments.”

Overall, Hale said she “expect(s) to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Sean Fergus, VP of Economic Research at builder-focused data and analytics firms NewHomeSource and Zonda, largely came to the same conclusion as Hale.

“Rates have since eased,” he said, “but buyers need to trust that relief will last before they come back in force.”

Yun had a more positive outlook, predicated on whether mortgage rates continue to decline. In NAR’s press release, he said that “(b)ased on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.”

Yun also commented on the relatively good financial position of homeowners currently, saying that they “are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation.”

As evidence for this claim, he pointed to the “historically low” number of distressed property sales, which “remains…at only 2% of all transactions.”

As a final sort of snapshot on the real estate ecosystem, total unsold inventory ticked up 1.3% to 1.59 million units, or the equivalent of 5.1 months’ supply. September 2026 recorded 4.7 months’ worth of unsold inventory, still higher than 4.4 months’ unsold inventory in October 2025, from which 1.59 million units represents a 4.6% yearly  increase.

Median existing-home sale prices increased more modestly, only crawling up 0.4% year-over-year to $416,700. The same median price was $414,900 last October. Even so, this is the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.
