#5590. Google retools Kubernetes for AI agents instead of building a new stack

Agentic workloads are pushing Kubernetes into territory its creators never planned for. Agents generate untrusted code on the fly, sit idle for long stretches and churn through pods at a pace that strains the orchestrator’s control plane.

Cloud providers are now rethinking how general-purpose a cluster should be. Google LLC’s answer is to stop treating every cluster as an infinitely flexible engine and tune each one into a runtime optimized for its workload, according to Jago Macleod (pictured, right), director of engineering for Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine at Google Cloud.

“There isn’t enough memory. There aren’t enough machines. So we have to get more efficient. And so one of the ways that we do that is to focus the Kubernetes cluster on the workload it’s running, and optimize it for that specific workload,” Macleod said.

Macleod and Jaana Dogan (pictured, left), principal engineer at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google is customizing Kubernetes for agentic workloads without fragmenting the open-source ecosystem. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes was built for microservices, then stretched to handle training jobs in which a single pod claims an entire node, Macleod explained. Agents are a different beast again, and some teams have resorted to building custom control planes just to cope.

“I think the agentic workloads are so different in the thrash and the churn that they represent is really not what we built Kubernetes for at all,” Macleod said. “And then agentic applications are almost the polar opposite, which is, you know, in the naive implementation, you just have as many pods as you can possibly fit, and so then the API machinery is running into limits.”

Platform teams have spent a decade making Kubernetes their compute fabric, and customers told Google they did not want agents to fragment it, Dogan explained. Google’s response is Agent Substrate, which runs AI agents in sandboxes directly on Kubernetes. The company donated the project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and recently released version 1.0. Because agents write their own code, that code is untrusted by default and needs sandboxing and network guardrails, according to Dogan. Customers also flagged a costly inefficiency.

“For example, our customers came to us, ‘Hey, majority of the time our agents are idle, but we have to allocate a sandbox all through the lifetime of a session,'” Dogan said. That means wasting a lot of CPU cycles, she explained.

Coding agents are also changing how engineers work, producing more prototypes and smaller, more focused teams, Dogan noted. As agentic workloads multiply, human judgment grows more valuable rather than less, according to Macleod.

“It’s not really, you know, fire off a prompt and forget it and walk away,” Macleod said. “It’s just a different level in the system where you’re applying your judgment and expertise. And that has never been more important.”

(* Disclosure: Google Cloud sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither Google Cloud nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5589. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

If you're active duty, you've served, or you know someone who has, connect with a local agent and a trusted VA-approved lender to see what you qualify for.Your VA home loan benefit and today's market could be a powerful combination.

#5588. Historic New England City Reclaims Top Spot as America’s Hottest Market

A Connecticut metro known for its insurance headquarters and the Pratt & Whitney aerospace company has reclaimed its title as America's hottest housing market.

The Hartford, CT, metro area has shot back to the No. 1 spot in October for the first time since a summer run at the top from May through July 2026, according to the Realtor.com® October Hottest Markets report. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, claiming the crown eight times.

The Nutmeg State accounts for four of the top 20 markets, with Waterbury, New Haven, and Norwich joining Hartford with median list prices between $400,000 and $460,000, says the report.

The No. 1 market encompasses the cities of Hartford, West Hartford, and East Hartford, but also a large swath of quintessential historical towns that look like they stepped out of a Hallmark movie.

Those small towns—including Wethersfield, Windsor Locks, Avon, and Farmington—draw homebuyers with their small-town charm, stunning nature, and commutable locations.

They also offer relative affordability compared to the elite suburbs dotting the Long Island Sound, such as Greenwich, Westport, and Darien, which are closer to New York City.

But Hartford, the state's capital, is still close enough that it embraces some spillover from the more expensive areas. If residents need to commute to New York City only a couple of times a week, the approximately 2.5-hour drive or Amtrak ride may be worth it for the nature, safety, quiet, and relative affordability these small towns offer.

"Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

And home browsers are most definitely interested.

The Hartford metro had 4.1 times the viewers per property as the rest of the country, by far the highest. Median days on the market are a swift 37 (only one more than last year and a month faster than the national time) and the median list price is $440,000, the second-highest among the top 10, behind only Manchester-Nashua, NH, at $549,000.

Homes in the most wanted markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on the market of 37 days, more than three weeks faster.

The hottest markets for October 2026 are Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (4.1 times the national average); Kenosha, WI (2.8); Lancaster, PA (2.4); Rochester, NY (2.5); Manchester-Nashua, NH (2.8); Peoria, IL (2.4); Erie, PA (2.8); Rockford, IL (2.6); and Waterbury-Shelton, CT (2.8).

Incorporated in 1693, Glastonbury (named after the town in England) boasts the country's oldest continuously running ferry, to Rocky Hill across the Connecticut River. It also has the second-highest concentration of surviving pre-1800s Colonial homes, about 154.

An easy 15-minute commute to Hartford via Route 2, and abutting both West Hartford and East Hartford, Glastonbury has long been a home base for the higher-ups in both the nearby insurance industry and Pratt & Whitney ("Pratt rats," in local lingo).

The past few decades have seen major changes for the formerly rural town as sprawling, multimillion-dollar estates began flecking the hills that were only farmland and tobacco fields not long ago.

Glastonbury has managed to retain much of its historical and rural appeal even as the town gained both a Whole Foods and a Trader Joe's, and its median home price skyrocketed, currently standing at $530,300, a 6.2% increase over last year.

Wendy Anderson of William Pitt Sotheby's International Realty, who represents the town's most expensive listing, a $7.2 million French chateau-style estate in South Glastonbury, says the town continues to draw high earners not only from Hartford, but from New York City and New Haven as well.

"It's always been a strong market, a sought-after town," she tells Realtor.com. "It's an easy commute."

Beyond the commute, the town—which is fairly large for a "small town" at about 52 square miles, with three ZIP codes—seems to have it all.

Beyond its bustling commercial center—complete with shops, restaurants, coffee spots, and an urgent care clinic—the area still boasts working farms, orchards, two active wineries, a sandy-shored pond, and a riverfront park.

All public schools have a rating of 8 or higher out of 10 by Great Schools, drawing families.

The housing stock is diverse: In addition to the aforementioned Colonial homes, there are small ranches, grand estates, classic midcentury homes, newer townhomes, and upscale rentals. There are even senior and lower-income communities.

"A lot of towns in Hartford County have a lot of amenities and activities," says Anderson, who has lived in Glastonbury for 45 years. "And a great sense of community. There's town football, soccer, tennis. So many activities for children, and concerts. And it's easy to get to the shoreline, or to get to Boston or New York."

Anderson doesn't think the market will go up indefinitely.

"I think the market has peaked, the wave has crested," she says. "But the market is still holding strong."

Since listing the $7.2 million French chateau on nearly 2 acres in July, she has already shown the estate to a dozen potential buyers—and just closed on a $1.4 million home that was sold in less than a week.

Buyers, usually business owners, are lured to the town by its spectacular fall colors, its rolling hills and dense forests, its fruit orchards, its gourmet restaurants and cosy taverns—as well as its relative affordability.

Adds the agent: "I just saw a TikTok video that said, 'This town, Glastonbury—it's like Greenwich, but half the price!'"

West of the river, a mere 10 miles away from Glastonbury, is West Hartford. An undercurrent of rivalry has long existed between West Hartford and Glastonbury, with both attracting Hartford's top earners from the healthcare, insurance, and education industries.

Although less than half the size of Glastonbury, West Hartford offers many of the same charms with its mix of idyllic small-town life and modern convenience.

Both towns are considered very walkable compared to the average Connecticut suburb, have highly rated public school systems, and have beautifully maintained their share of pre-1800s historic homes.

West Hartford, however, tends to be more expensive at its high end, standing at a median of $712,000 for its 06107 ZIP code, a slight dip from last year.

Robert Levine of ERA Real Estate, who lives and sells in West Hartford and the surrounding areas, says the two upscale suburbs have a few key differences.

Glastonbury has larger plot sizes, with homes often sitting on an acre or more of land, and has room to grow. West Hartford, a more suburban enclave with no real room left to build, has a denser, more bustling center of town.

"We're a destination. People come from 15 miles away to have dinner in our center," Levine says.

As for the metro being the hottest one in the country, the agent says he isn't surprised—he still sees multiple offers on turnkey homes that check all the boxes: good location, backyard, basement, two-car garage, etc.

But he declares that the area is in a "transitional market," with some homes sitting for several months.

"Homeowners are scratching their heads, like, 'Wait, my home won't sell in a weekend?'" he says.

"We're transitioning to what I call an 'equilibrium' market," he adds. "It's not necessarily favorable to either buyers or sellers. It's all about the property."

As for why central Connecticut keeps luring buyers, the agent notes the scenery, the small-town vibes combined with modern ease, and the tight-knit communities.

#5587. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5585. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. And that means less rushing, fewer last-minute surprises, and a better chance to make a great first impression when you're ready to sell.Thinking about selling in 2027? #5584. 4 insights from Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026: AI agents join the team as working colleagues

At Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026, AI agents moved out of single-player chat windows and into shared workspaces. There they work beside people as named, auditable members of the team. Block Inc. built these tools to run itself as an intelligence company, and it is now offering them to other businesses, building on Buzz, its open-source workspace for humans and AI agents. Block introduced Builderlab as a set of tools for teams and AI agents to work together.

The next phase will depend less on how capable a single agent becomes than on how well agents collaborate, share an organization’s context and stay inside firm security boundaries. Block plans to spread that model with open-source code, model-agnostic design and hosted infrastructure. The company is making that push while its core business delivers a third straight guidance raise.

“If you’re talking about making the whole organization more productive, you need to break down these distinctions between what the software does and what the people do,” said Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

Alison Kosik (left) and co-host Gillin spoke with industry experts during Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026 in San Francisco. The interviews covered Block’s open-source business model, agents with their own identities, the shift from prompting to overnight delegation and the security controls that let enterprises trust autonomous systems. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are four standout insights from the event:

Builderlab gives developers endlessly customizable agents on an open-source plug-in architecture, and the launch audience of application builders cheered the idea, according to Gillin. Agents in Buzz have names, avatars and personalities. That shifts the focus from switching among software-as-a-service applications to the work itself, and it could threaten SaaS companies. The revenue model follows the classic open-source pattern of giving the software away and charging for the convenience of a hosted cloud service, he explained. Block said little about commercialization or about Cash App, which brings in 60% of its revenue, according to Gillin.

Most AI tools are built for one person at a time, so each user becomes the bottleneck when results have to be shared with a team, noted Lucas Isaza, product lead of Buzz at Block. In Buzz, agents have their own identities, can be tagged like colleagues and leave an audit trail of every action. Plug-ins, added after the first version launched in July, let anyone reshape the interface. Nontechnical staff, such as account managers building personal dashboards, have been the heaviest users of the companion apps platform. Companies can self-host the open-source code, use a free tier or add funds for remote agents, models and extra storage, Isaza highlighted.

Builderlab sits as an interface layer above the models, so Buzz can use agents from any AI lab and switch to the newest frontier model as it arrives, emphasized Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block. Remote agents run in central cloud environments that are easier to secure than laptops. People can hand them large assignments overnight and act as reviewers. Instead of soft guardrails, agents run on secure building blocks that never grant them permission for certain actions. Some teams have shipped software releases 50% to 75% faster. Axen expects agents to need much less human steering within the next year because they already sit inside the conversation.

Securing agents that act on their own does not mean starting over, because principles such as least privilege, isolated environments and egress controls still apply, shared James Nettesheim, chief information security officer and head of enterprise technology at Block. Builderlab gives every agent a full identity owned by a human, runs it in hardened cloud virtual machines and records its actions in a cryptographically signed ledger that cannot be altered. Block is also building information flow control, which tags data from sensitive sources so the security policy travels with that data and blocks leaks. AI already reviews Block’s code and sorts its security alerts. Nettesheim added that agents let defenders keep pace with attackers’ machine speed.

#5583. A New Wave of Opportunity Zones Is Coming in 2027—and Home Values Are Already Surging in Key States

The United States has thousands of new Opportunity Zones, a designation that could bring rising values to many emerging housing markets.

The Treasury Department last week announced 6,576 new Opportunity Zones (OZ), which will maintain that status for the next decade. All 50 states and the District of Columbia have zones in the mix, and 2,594 of them are in rural areas. OZs benefit from enhanced economic incentives, and they're targeted at communities with the potential to grow.

“By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

This is the second round of OZs since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act established the program in 2017. The private sector has invested $110 billion in developing the first crop, Treasury said. The original OZs remain active through 2028, and the new ones begin in 2027. Some OZs were renewed.

States submitted nominations from about 25,300 census tracts eligible for the program, and leaders cheered their wins. There are about 25% fewer tracts than last time.

"Whether it's bringing new life to a downtown, creating great-paying jobs, or building housing for more families, these Opportunity Zones will help attract investments that can make a real difference in the lives of Ohioans," Gov. Mike DeWine said of Ohio's 260 new OZs.

“Virginia is ready to harness the potential of Opportunity Zones,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said of the state's 153 new OZs. “I worked closely with local leaders across Virginia to make sure we supported the priorities that mattered most to local communities."

Property data group ATTOM analyzed 3,805 OZ census tracts from the last tranche and found median single-family home and condo prices rose in 48.1% them. Compare that to home prices outside of OZs, which rose 51.6%.

Some OZs see their home values rise much more quickly. ATTOM found that about 9.4% of the OZ census tracts saw their highest median home value since the Great Recession in the third quarter of 2026. About 27.1% of them saw double-digit growth in home values year over year.

“Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80% of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so, home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.”

As far as states with a lot of OZ price growth, Maine came in first, with 64% of its OZs seeing median home prices rise. South Carolina (61.3%), Wisconsin (58.3%), Virginia (53%), and Oregon (52.3%) rounded out the top five.

ATTOM noted that many of the census tracts recorded a low number of sales, so the data can be volatile. Still, 79.5% of them had home prices below the national median. Outside of them, just 50.4% of tracts had prices below the national median.

Michael Tillman, CEO of OZ developer PTM Partners, tells Realtor.com® the program also gives developers time to experiment. His company builds workforce housing in Florida using cold-formed steel and vertical integration.

"These are not build-and-flip products; we want to be there as their family grows," Tillman said of the units. "That's stickier than high-end luxury. There's got to be more institutional capital with that long-term focus."

OZs tend to have higher poverty rates, lower median family income, and more housing cost burdens than a typical area. Some are in urban areas, and others are in rural ones.

Brookings Institute analyzed the OZ program and found half of the zones saw "accelerated growth." But it said the designation alone doesn't create success. Local market conditions and state and local regulations play a role. And, while they do often mean new investment, that can vary depending on the development already there.

"Investment alone is not synonymous with shared prosperity," Brookings said in the report. "In some places, OZ capital has expanded housing supply, supported business formation, created jobs, and leveraged underutilized community assets—while in others, it flowed toward projects with limited community benefits or into neighborhoods already on a growth path."

Brookings also noted the first round of OZs came when the country already saw increased building. What this means in the current, challenged market has yet to be seen. States should develop a strategy for how to develop each zone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5582. Inside the $3.25 Million Pasadena Glass Pavilion That’s Still Studied in Architecture Classes Today

A three-bedroom midcentury modern home designed by Case Study architect Craig Ellwood has just come on the market in Pasadena, CA, for $3.25 million. It features a notable cantilevered glass pavilion.

Built in 1965, the Kubly House was originally constructed for less than $45,000. The 2,227-square-foot home has since been thoughtfully updated.

“What makes this house special is its architecture and design, and how true it has remained to the original,” says Chris Suarez, who is co-listing the property with Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass. “Nothing was significantly altered. Everything done was intended to restore the house to its original condition. The footprint, the floors, the glass—everything has remained true to the original design.”

Located in the Linda Vista neighborhood, the home has an iconic redwood, cantilevered glass pavilion that opens to a single-level floor plan. The private half-acre lot includes a pool and spa surrounded by lush landscaping with eucalyptus and oak trees.

With exposed post-and-beam construction, clean horizontal lines, and expansive walls of glass, the home was designed to give the illusion of floating above its natural surroundings. The deck was recently restored using specially milled wood.

“It was sourced from northern Washington and brought down here,” Suarez notes. “Everything was done painstakingly to avoid altering the house’s integrity, architecture, and design. That being said, significant work has been done, including updates to the roof, infrastructure, air conditioning, and electrical systems. All the major systems have been updated, but you wouldn’t necessarily know it because the work was done so carefully.”

Originally commissioned by ArtCenter College of Design alumni and educators Don and Sally Kubly, the home represents their understanding of design and the culture of the college community. It is still studied in classes there.

“Don was ArtCenter’s first president in Pasadena,” Suarez explains. “There’s also a connection through Craig Ellwood, who designed ArtCenter’s main campus building. The main campus is an incredible steel-and-glass building designed by Ellwood. Don played a significant role in moving the school from Los Angeles to Pasadena, where he served as president for many years. He’s very well known within that community, and this house is significant to the college’s history and culture.”

Based on available architectural records, the Kubly House is said to be Ellwood’s only documented residential project in Pasadena.

After remaining in the Kubly family for nearly six decades, the home changed hands for $3.6 million in 2022. Since then, the sellers have undertaken a preservation-minded restoration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction, updating major systems to contemporary standards.

“A house that helped usher in much midcentury modernism was the Glass House, designed by Philip Johnson around 1948 or 1949,” Benz notes. “That design was definitely something Ellwood loved. You can clearly see that house’s influence here, which is important because it reveals some of the influences behind Ellwood’s work.”

Benz adds that the home’s design was also influenced by Ellwood’s peers, including midcentury designer George Nelson.

“A furniture plan developed for the house clearly referenced Mies van der Rohe and George Nelson, both important figures in midcentury modern design,” she says. “Even the deck and the steps leading to the house resemble a George Nelson bench. There’s actually a bench built into the concrete wall near the pool that resembles a George Nelson design. I don’t know whether Nelson designed or made it, but the influence is certainly there.”

The house is special because many of the original details have remained intact, she adds.

“You can see the influence of the people Ellwood admired throughout the house,” Benz says. “That significance is what makes this house important when you look at the midcentury modernist movement. All these examples are visible in the house and remain there.”

Some of the built-in furniture has a distinctive style, too.

“There’s a stunning floating credenza that looks like a George Nelson piece,” she notes. “We think it might be one of his designs. It’s in the living room. There’s also a built-in console that might be a George Nelson design as well. So, some of the furniture is actually built into the architecture.”

While some pieces are originals and others are reproductions, Benz says, “the most important thing was following the original plan. The history of this house is everything.”

When staging the home, she says they were “fortunate to discover an original interior design study among the blueprints, plans, and documents that came with the house. We were able to look at that study, and it became a guide and a road map for staging the property. Sourcing the furniture was a challenge because we had to find the specific pieces.”

The city of Pasadena has also identified the property as eligible for individual listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

#5581. Rates Come Down Again but Remain Over 7%

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates eased again for the fourth-straight week but remain almost a full percentage point over last year at this time, a key reason buyers continue to hold back and why the market remains sluggish.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.11%, down seven bases points from  7.18% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.24% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.45%, down from 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%.

At presstime, the average rate was back up to 7.42% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said that while rates are at their lowest level since late September, borrowing costs are still nearly a full percentage point higher than they were last year at this time.

“While rates have declined for three weeks in a row, homebuyers are still holding back,” Sturtevant said in a statement. “Higher rates, along with on-going economic uncertainty, are key reasons why housing market activity is so sluggish this fall.

She also said there is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year, and that, given this week’s inflation report, it’s more likely for rates to increase instead.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines,” she said. “In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets. Inventory is rising but higher rates are causing sellers to pause along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly even if rates move higher.”

Sturtevant noted that data on pending home sales suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the fourth quarter. “It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jiayi Xu added that the recent downtrend trend with rates could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%.

“The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike,” Xu said in a statement. “On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast.”

Xu also said today’s homebuyers are being squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, with inflation being the bigger long-term problem.

“High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are,” she said. “But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.”

#5580. Paris Signal Week looks to bridge crypto and institutional finance

Paris Blockchain Week is now Signal Week, a reflection of cryptocurrency’s global expansion.

The newly rebranded event is joining forces with RAISE Summit, the annual AI and networking conference, and Machina Summit, Europe’s leading physical AI event. Event organizers expect approximately 2,500 attendees, highlighting the growing profile of blockchain technology.

“The industry has changed a lot,” said Michael Amar (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week. “We really want to be the place where we bridge traditional finance and digital assets. It’s where the market is finally, and we are embracing it completely. We have the desire to go abroad to launch other conferences. So it made sense that … we join everything under the same roof, but different flows, different marketing and different ticketing.”

Amar and Charlie Meraud (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week, spoke with theCUBE host Gemma Allen, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed what to expect at the 2027 event and the evolution of cryptocurrency. (* Disclosure below.)

Signal Week is designed to cover the intersection between institutional finance and digital assets. Since its founding, the crypto market has grown to $40 billion in tokenized real-world assets, or RWA, according to Meraud. The week will also encompass the CXO Summit, a private gathering of C-suite executives.

“The CXO Summit is organizing a roundtable under Chatham House rules with these … crypto-native players discussing all sophisticated topics around what they are building and how they can partner all year long,” he said. “This is the kind of activation that makes people book a flight, buy a ticket and come to Signal Week. The industry needed a room for these players to connect and start actually doing business.”

Both founders see facilitating conversations between crypto leaders and traditional finance executives as one of the primary goals of the conference. The chief executive officers of Kaiko, Morpho and Fireblocks, all leading digital asset companies, are expected to attend. European Union regulators will also be present, Amar and Meraud emphasize, which will be critical for understanding the future of AI-powered finance.

“We’re creating those moments where people can get the most out of the conference,” Amar said. “If you talk about the C-suite, people coming from traditional finance and meeting the makers of the crypto industry, we’re creating the space where they will have talks in a very small room where actually we go very much into the details of the use cases of the implementation of a digital asset solution for a bank, for example.”

Another key topic at Signal Week and RAISE Summit will be custody, the safekeeping of private keys that allow a person to prove they control an address and the cryptocurrency it holds. Security has long been a divisive issue for cryptocurrency, spurring a variety of solutions.

“When we started … self-custody was one of the promised digital assets,” Meraud said. “A lot of players have been offering different ways of custodying digital assets. And having the most sophisticated solution coming to Signal Week, explaining all the new features, they’ve been building over the years is one of the reasons financial institutions are willing to connect and network with our audience.”

#5579. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.11% Rate

Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac. Even with this steady month-long decline, borrowing costs remain significantly higher than they were a year ago, when rates averaged 6.24% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,314. This reflects a $16 monthly reduction from the previous week’s payment of $2,330.

Compared to the 6.24% average from November 2025, which required a $2,116 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $198 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,791.

This reflects a $20 decrease from last week's monthly cost of $2,811. Compared to the 6.24% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,552, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $239 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $193 in relative relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this continued downward drift improves overall borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.11% rate will pay a total of $833,080 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage. While current financing costs remain elevated compared to year-ago levels, this total still represents a distinct contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $57,550 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.11% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,004,902 for principal and interest. If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $69,421 for FHA buyers.

While stubborn inflation may limit how much further rates can fall in the weeks ahead, this four-week pullback has helped trim monthly expenses for buyers jumping in the late-fall market.

#5578. Kubernetes gets a second act as AI agents turn one prompt into thousands of inference calls

The rise of agentic AI systems is giving Kubernetes, long valued for its reliability and predictability, an unexpected second act.

As AI spending shifts from training models toward serving them and running agents, the open-source community is developing tools to handle the growing volume of inference requests. The orchestration platform was built from the start for dynamic, distributed workloads, which gave fast-growing AI companies a reliable foundation, according to Jonathan Bryce (pictured), executive director of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

“The AI boom has sparked a massive investment and a huge build-out of infrastructure overall,” Bryce said. “Having Kubernetes built from the beginning to handle really dynamic distributed workloads as those companies were growing like crazy — they had a really reliable, solid foundation to build on at the same time.”

Bryce spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how CNCF projects can meet rising inference demand, make better use of data center hardware and secure AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

New models grab headlines with benchmark scores in math and software engineering. But a model has no value until it can be served at high performance, and early chatbots made that look simple because each message triggered a single inference call, Bryce explained. Agents can make repeated inference calls to complete a single task, a shift the CNCF has put on the KubeCon agenda with its new AI inference and agentic track.

“We’re using coding agents to say, ‘Build me a system that does this,’ and it’ll spawn 10 sub-agents,” Bryce said. “Each of those are doing thousands of inference calls over the course of hours and just churning away.”

As inference demand fuels a data center construction boom and raises local concerns about resource use, the llm-d inference engine and Agent Substrate, which offers compact hosting for long-running agents, aim to get more performance out of existing hardware, Bryce said. Security and control pose another challenge because agents can make different choices when given the same task. OpenShell, a security project now under the CNCF’s neutral governance following Nvidia Corp.’s contribution, drew more than 300 contributing companies within months, a milestone which might once have taken two years to reach, he added.

“What I am constantly thinking about is, ‘How do we lower friction to collaboration?'” Bryce said. “How do we enable people to be able to move at the pace that the world and the industry is moving at, and how do we, while doing that, continue to drive that into collaboration around open solutions that can become those base and infrastructure components that we can all build on?”

#5577. Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. She is reportedly suspected of facilitating Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies. The investigation has raised concerns about potential Chinese intelligence involvement and whether Nvidia’s technology reached restricted customers.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

A second relationship emerged through a New York Times report identifying Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell reportedly worked directly under Huang, creating additional corporate governance questions.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. Directors previously expressed confidence in Huang, but Bloomberg subsequently reported that Nvidia had engaged an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. Losing Huang would remove the founder most closely associated with its AI dominance, potentially forcing investors to reassess the company’s leadership and long-term strategy.

The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.

#5576. Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results

Shares of artificial intelligence cloud operator Nebius Holdings NV dropped 17% today after it posted third-quarter financial results.

The company’s adjusted profit and revenue topped expectations. The selloff may have been sparked by its full-year forecast, which fell short of the consensus estimate. It’s also possible the sudden departure of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed. Nvidia is an investor in Nebius and many other AI and cloud companies.

Another possible factor: Nebius increased its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion. According to CNBC, that’s $4.15 billion higher than what Wall Street had expected. The company’s plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year surpassed the consensus estimate by an even wider margin.

The surging expenses may be related to its shift away from colocation facilities. Today, about 90% of the company’s infrastructure is located in rented data centers. In contrast, the next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity that it plans to bring online will be mostly powered by internally operated data centers.

“Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term,” said founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh. “We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure buildout, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market.”

Nebius swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year ago to a $90.9 million adjusted profit. The latter figure breaks down to adjusted earnings of 31 cents per share. The company’s profitability surprised analysts, who expected a loss of 69 cents per share.

Revenue growth was another bright spot. Sales jumped 517% year-over-year, to $980.8 million, which put the company well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus estimate.

One of Nebius’ main growth drivers is its Token Factory service for running open-source AI models. Developers use it to host both post-training and inference workloads. Nebius says that the offering, which launched a year ago, is nearing a “multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate” after logging a 17-fold quarter-over-increase in contract value.

Nebius’ largest customers played a particularly important role in its strong quarterly performance. The company signed $12 billion worth of contracts in the three months ended Sept. 30. The haul included multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and other major tech firms.

The company uses customers’ contract prepayments to finance its data center projects. The company says that the value of the prepayments it received in the third quarter exceeded its capital expenditures. However, the ratio of prepayments to capital expenditures is expected to decline as Nebius ramps up its data center spending. That detail may be yet another factor in today’s stock selloff.

Nebius expects its full-year revenue to be “at the low end” of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range. Analysts expected $3.37 billion. For 2027, Nebius is forecasting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue.

#5575. 5 Converted Schoolhouses and Banks You Can Buy Right Now, Priced Below $400K

If you've ever dreamed of owning a charming piece of history and transforming it into the home of your dreams, a former bank or schoolhouse might be just the opportunity you've been waiting for.

Not only do these unique properties offer a place to call home but they also provide a chance to preserve a piece of the past while creating something entirely your own.

Full of charm, character, and possibilities, these structures feature many original details, including vintage bank vaults and architectural details.

From Maine to Wisconsin, we found five converted banks and schoolhouses priced below $400,000 that offer a unique opportunity to live somewhere with a story to tell.

CSAA Landmark Schoolhouse: Built in 1865, this 600-square-foot building has been converted into a stylish one-bedroom, loft-style home.

The charming open floor plan has hardwood floors and a cozy living room that flows into the dining area and kitchen. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, which have vaulted wood ceilings. Recent improvements include energy-efficient hydronic baseboard heating.

A garden, an oversized shed, and a hot tub are also on the wooded lot.

Michele M. Barry of Lake Lady Property Management is the listing agent.

Former Stayton School: Set on 3 acres, this 4,000-square-foot building has 1,400 square feet of finished living space. It comes with unfinished space for the next buyer to remodel.

Built in 1946, the home features many original details, including preserved hardwood floors, custom millwork, oversized windows, and high ceilings. The living room still has a chalkboard lining the wall, and wall-mounted water fountains nod to the building’s past. The updated kitchen has custom cabinetry and a farmhouse sink. An original raised “performance stage” could be used for entertaining or converted into a studio.

Donna Piehl of Realty Executives Hometown Living is the listing agent.

Former Stockton Springs High School: Built in 1880, this 6,244-square-foot former schoolhouse serves as a blank canvas. It could be transformed into a one-of-a-kind residence, a multipurpose retreat, or an event space.

Many original features remain, including tile, wood, and vinyl flooring. The generously sized rooms offer endless possibilities for entertaining, workshops, gatherings, or other uses (subject to town approval). Some interior improvements have already been completed, while other projects have been started, giving the next owner a head start on bringing their vision to life. An unfinished lower level provides even more room for expansion and customization.

It is located nearby Stockton Springs Harbor, which flows into Penobscot Bay.

Keirsten Wyman of Re/Max Jaret & Cohn is the listing agent.

Former First National Bank of Pennsylvania: This former financial institution offers more than 5,000 square feet of versatile commercial space, which could be used for offices, retail shops, or a fitness center, with appropriate approvals.

Built in 1901, this property features a vintage bank vault, original ATM, night-deposit box, glass block windows, and private offices. Recent improvements include updated bathrooms featuring luxury vinyl flooring, modern lighting, and new vanities. The lower level has a kitchenette, meeting area, storage space, media room, and high-end carpeting.

The layout also offers the potential to rent out individual offices and generate additional income.

Stephanie Ramer of eXp Realty is the listing agent.

Country schoolhouse: Built in 1927, this brick structure has been transformed into a 952-square-foot cabin.

The one-room dwelling has hardwood floors, a custom-detailed ceiling, and numerous windows. An unfinished lower level offers an opportunity for future expansion. A covered deck overlooks the private lot.

According to the listing, the property, "ready for its next chapter," could be used as a primary residence, weekend retreat, or hunting cabin.

Tina Attoe of Beiser Realty is the listing agent.

#5574. Realty Executives Associates Appoints New Executive Vice President of Agent Development

Realty Executives Associates (REA) has announced the appointment of J Lewis as executive vice president of Agent Development, a newly established leadership role focused on strengthening the success, productivity and long-term relationships of REA’s agents.

According to a release, prior to joining REA, Lewis served as CEO of Keller Williams for 13 years, bringing extensive experience in brokerage leadership, agent development and organizational growth.

In this new role, the company says Lewis will focus on helping existing agents increase productivity and profitability, strengthening agent relationships and retention and creating meaningful opportunities for professional development and business growth. He will work to provide agents with the resources, guidance and support they need to build sustainable businesses.

“One of the things I enjoy most is sitting down with an agent or a team, understanding what they’re trying to accomplish, and helping them figure out how to get there. That might mean looking at their production data, analyzing their financials, identifying opportunities they’re not seeing, or simply fine-tuning the way they run their business,” he says. “Every agent has different goals, and I enjoy helping them develop a plan to reach those goals and build a business that supports the life they want.”

“I’m incredibly excited to join the number one brokerage in East Tennessee,” Lewis added. “What really attracted me to REA is the opportunity to work with a company that understands the value of investing in its people. I’ve always enjoyed working alongside agents, understanding what they want to accomplish, and helping them find ways to get there. REA has created an environment where that kind of work is valued, and I’m excited to be part of it.”

“At REA, we believe our agents are our customers. Our responsibility is to create an environment where they can build successful, sustainable businesses and feel supported along the way. This position is an extension of that commitment,” said Justin Bailey, CEO and partner of Realty Executives Associates.

Bailey added: “Success isn’t simply measured by how many agents we have. It’s measured by the success of the agents who choose to call REA home. We want to be intentional about helping them become more productive, more profitable, and better positioned for the future. We have always believed that taking care of our people is what makes a great brokerage, and this is another way we are putting that belief into action.”

For more information, visit www.realtyexecutives.com.

#5573. 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle

The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.

For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.

“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”

Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:

Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.

At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.

Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.

At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.

Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.

Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

#5572. Detached Home in Desirable DC Neighborhood Gets Major Discount—and the Photos Hide a Wild Catch

A Washington, DC, home has been put on the market for far under the area’s median listing price, but the reason is buried within the listing—and online forums are not happy about it.

At first glance, 1007 Evarts St NE is a stunning six-bed, five-bath home, with a jaw dropping $375,000 price tag, nearly 40% below the zip code’s median listing price of $607,500.

The first nine photos on the listing show an updated, bright, and beautifully staged home with a perfectly manicured lawn. But flip to the tenth photo, and the image changes. The rest of the photos show a smaller home, stripped to the studs and in need of complete rehabilitation, both inside and out.

The key detail then becomes clear: a watermark reading “Architect’s rendering—not an actual photo” in the corner of the listing’s primary photos.

The property details tell the rest of the story.

“Much of the pre-construction work is already done. Demolition is complete and the structure is down to a clean shell with the framing exposed,” the property details read. “The sale includes a DC-approved plan set for a full rebuild. The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.”

Investors, developers, and 203(k) rehab buyers who want to skip design stage and jump right into construction are the ideal buyers, according to the listing.

With that information taken into consideration, the severe price reduction from the area’s norm listing makes sense.

However, the listing has still received heat online, where one Threads user reposted the images with the caption, “This has got to be the most click bait home ive ever seen…..this gotta be illegal, right?”

The replies are filled with equally outraged users.

“Is that AI renderings of potential build and then the actual pics of an as-is shack???” wrote another user.

“The listing is deceptive because you don’t know what you’re looking at. I certainly don’t. And you’re right, you can’t advertise potential. It’s absolutely unethical,” wrote one user, who identified herself as a real estate agent. “The architect rendered pics should have never been included. Those would easily be shown separately to a potential buyer. If you’re selling a clean shell, that’s all that should be pictured.”

The listing did have one defender in the replies: the home’s listing agent, Tohmai Smith. He argued that all of the necessary information is available in the listing, and if he was trying to deceive buyers, pictures of the house as-is wouldn’t have been included.

“It’s in the description: ‘The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.’ And they’re not AI. A licenses architect built them from the DC-approved plans, which convey with the sale,” Smith wrote. “The finished home is a $1.3M house. The $400K buys you the shell, the approved plans and a head start.”

Users continued to question his claim that the photos weren’t made with AI, pointing out discrepancies in the rendered photos and structural issues with the back staircase as potential clues that they weren’t made with professional architectural programs.

Others questioned the possibility of fitting a six-bed, five-bath home on the moderate 5,066-square-foot lot.

In subsequent replies, Smith explained the use of 203(k) loans to both buy a home and finance the renovation in one mortgage and further argued that the purpose of the renderings is to show buyers the home’s potential. Within these posts, he invited interested parties or those with questions to send him a direct message.

“Without these renderings, how would a buyer know what’s possible? Even after seeing them, people can’t believe it,” Smith wrote. “But it IS possible, and that’s exactly why I show them.”

Bright MLS, which is responsible for listings in the Mid-Atlantic region and carries the Evarts Street listing, has a rule that any “Virtually Staged” images must be labeled, and no AI alterations can alter permanent features or hide defects, according to Imagen for Real Estate.

Another law has been proposed in Washington DC to require listings to disclose any photo editing and include both unedited photos and a written list of all changes.

Despite online controversy, the listing for 1007 Evarts Street NE appears to follow both the active and proposed guidelines, by including actual photos of the property and describing the state of the home in the property details section.

Realtor.com reached out to both Smith and Bright MLS for comments on the use of renderings in listings, but received no response at the time of publication.

#5571. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.
